query.query: A quiet background pytest log looks stuck. How do I tell whether my run is still progressing?

labelled it **elapsed**. `%Y` is mtime, so it is log *staleness*. It read "11 min" on a run that
was 25 minutes old, and staleness on a quiet ingest phase looks exactly like a young run.

## 🔁 Second instance, 2026-09-01: `gh run watch`, and this time the file was NOT empty

Same false green, different tool, and the new detail is that **the output file looked healthy**.

`gh run list ... | xargs gh run watch <id> --exit-status`, backgrounded, notified "completed
(exit code 0)" with a **950-byte** output file full of green ticks. It contained exactly two
jobs, `typecheck` and `Schema migrations (PostgreSQL 16)`, then `[exited with code 0]`. The three
jobs that actually matter here, `test`, `floor` and `Clean install (wizard)`, were still pending
when the watch exited and appear nowhere in it. The watcher had attached to a partial view and
returned.

- **xdist replaces a crashed worker.** I asked for `-n 2` and the log named gw0 to gw9, which
  looked like the flag was ignored. It was not: workers kept dying and being replaced until xdist
  gave up. A worker count in the log that exceeds the one you passed is itself the symptom.
- **The cause was `Windows fatal exception: stack overflow`**, reproduced on a two-file slice
  seconds later. So it is the environment, not the suite, and CLAUDE.md's advice to run `-n 4` is
  currently unusable on this box. Dated because it may be as transient as the pyarrow Smart App
  Control block: re-measure with `python -m pytest tests/test_current_state.py -q -n 2`.

Observed 2026-08-23 in the recall worktree. A full test suite launched as a harness background
task "completed (exit code 0)" after ~10 minutes with an output file containing only
`[exited with code 0]`, no pytest output at all. The process was still alive (found later by
`Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` matching the exact command line) and kept writing to a database.
Trusting the notification and relaunching produced TWO concurrent suites against one session DB,
whose global-table tests interfere; both had to be killed and one clean run started.

1. **Is the process there at all?** `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='python.exe'"`
   with the command line printed. Match YOUR argv: on this machine there were **five concurrent
   pytest runs** from other sessions, so "a pytest is running" proves nothing about yours.
2. **Is it working or blocked?** Sample the CPU counter twice:
   `$p = Get-Process -Id <pid>; $p.CPU; Start-Sleep 20; $p.Refresh(); $p.CPU`. Mine went 995s to
   1002s in 20 wall seconds: alive, and starved to a third of a core by the other four suites.
3. Only then consider the output file.

**How to apply:** never end a backgrounded run with `| tail`. Write the full output and read the
tail of the FILE, or use `tee`. Reserve `tail` for foreground commands whose output you want
trimmed. And before restarting anything long, check liveness by process and CPU, because a restart
under contention costs the whole elapsed run and lands in the same queue.

⚠️ This machine routinely has several sessions running the full suite at once. A 30 to 40 minute
suite is a 51 minute suite under four-way contention, and that is not a regression to investigate.

See [[a-frozen-script-is-not-a-reproduction-pointer]] for what that run was verifying.

- **Log to a file on that host and follow the file.** `exec >>"$LOG" 2>&1` on the remote side, then
  `tail -f` from here. Killing the follower then changes nothing about the run, which is the honest
  arrangement given the work detaches whether you meant it to or not.
- **Start it detached deliberately** (`setsid`, stdin from `/dev/null`), so the shell detaches too
  rather than only the payload.
- **Stop it by the pid it recorded when it took its lock**, never by pattern. `pkill -f
  'bin/index_memory.sh'` also matches the ssh child carrying that string in its own command line, so
  it kills the connection before it can report. That happened here, once, and looked like the host
  had gone away.
- **Ask the DATABASE for progress**, not the log, when checking on a run somebody else

Back to [MEMORY.md](MEMORY.md) and [feedback_index.md](feedback_index.md).

**Cost, 2026-08-23: about an hour, and one suite run killed for no reason.** I launched
`pytest tests/ -q 2>&1 | tail -25` in the background, watched the output file sit at 188 bytes for
half an hour, read that as a slow suite, then as a hang, and restarted it. The second run sat at
184 bytes for 51 minutes and finished green: **6539 passed, 34 skipped in 51:33**.

**Why:** `tail -N` cannot emit anything until its input closes, so a pipeline that ends in `tail`
produces exactly zero incremental output no matter how healthy the run is. Nothing about the file
distinguishes "slow", "hung" and "dead".

block with the condition that clears it, and date one against the world before believing it.
- [A missing input becomes a clean null](missing-input-becomes-a-clean-null.md) — `.get(k, default)` in measurement code turns an absent field into a constant, and a constant scores as an ordinary negative result. The tell is a metric landing on the null value EXACTLY.
- [Detached runs need setsid, not nohup](detached-runs-need-setsid.md) — `nohup cmd &` from an SSH session still takes the HUP; and a rising row count proves a job WAS running, never that it still is. Check the checkpoint mtime.
- [An empty log is not completion](empty-log-is-not-completion.md) — I called a running job finished on a 0-byte log and a missing pid file; buffered stdout under nohup keeps the log empty for the WHOLE run.

**And the first run really was dead**, which is what made the wrong reading so comfortable: the
task had vanished from the harness's registry and no matching process existed. Two different
causes, one identical symptom, and the symptom is the thing I was watching.

## How to tell the three apart, in order of cost

Adjacent, same session, same lesson about verification steps that quietly lie: a Bash `&&` chain
short-circuited at a failed `git rev-parse`, so the `git log` behind my "fully pushed" claim never
ran, while a trailing `; echo` still printed the reassuring message. Conclusion happened to be
right, evidence was absent. Sibling of the standing rule never to read an exit code through a pipe
([[project-recall-store-latency-share-redis-nogo-2026-08-04]]). **Run a verification command
standalone and read its own exit code; never let a chain decide whether your check executed.**

Context: [[project-recall-mtrag-symmetric-baseline-2026-08-04]].

1. **Wait on the CONDITION, not the clock.** The replacement probe loops until `records >= 60`,
   re-checking that the process is alive each pass, so it cannot report a pre-ingest state as a
   state. A fixed sleep against a job whose phases have no fixed length is a coin flip.
2. **Alive is not working.** Having confirmed the process existed, I nearly stopped. `ps -o
   times` twice, 45 seconds apart, showed CPU climbing 156s (~350%, multi-threaded) and the HNSW
   `.bin` files growing: that is the evidence of progress. `pgrep` returning a pid is not.

**Those two lines are the expected-output comment inside a bash script template. The article prints
no results table.** My first reading of it reported them as measured per-condition scores, which is
wrong in the direction that makes the post look more empirical than it is. There is no dataset, no
linked raw output, and no run record.

To his credit he does not overclaim in prose: he states it is still one user, that every figure
comes from his own corpus, and that he cannot yet tell whether the result generalises. He discloses
that he builds cachly, at the end of the article. So this is an honest vendor essay, not a
disguised benchmark, and it should be described that way rather than attacked as one.

## Why it is not evidence in this benchmark's sense

`python -m pytest -q` on RE-call took **705 s (11m45s)** on this machine on 2026-08-08, finishing
3259 passed / 26 skipped with the pgvector container up. The comment beside `timeout = 120` in
`pyproject.toml` says "the whole suite runs in ~3 minutes"; that is stale and I should not plan
around it.

**Why:** I ran it in the foreground with the Bash tool's 600 s ceiling and it was force-backgrounded
mid-run. That is recoverable but it splits the turn and costs a round trip.

**How to apply:** run the full suite with `run_in_background: true` from the start, and keep
foreground runs to individual files. The per-test `timeout = 120` still applies, so a genuine hang
fails one test rather than the job.

🔑 **The test that would have caught this is a COUNT, not a shape.** The suite is ~7,100 tests;
any summary line whose passed+failed+skipped total is not in that ballpark is a non-run however
well formed it looks. CLAUDE.md already says "read the skip count before calling a run green" for
the 34-versus-several-hundred case; the same arithmetic catches this one, and it is the only rule
in this memo that does.

- **Always `--pool-size 4`** for backfill and launch runs. Direct connection mode loses the local
  Postgres connection during sparse backfill, because cursor reads and sparse writes share one held
  connection.
- **Never run the full SPLADE arm on local Windows CPU.** About 20 minutes for 1,227 chunks, so a
  500K-document corpus needs a rented GPU and a backgrounded launch.
- **Indexing progress is invisible to SQL while the process runs.** External counts returned zero
  even as the log printed `index wrote ...`. Trust `tail -f` on the run log, not a `SELECT count(*)`.
- **Throughput reference:** roughly 1,000 to 1,125 chunks/minute on both boxes, so full dense
  indexing is a 9 to 10 hour job before GPU SPLADE backfill even starts. Budget accordingly.
- `k=8` matched `k=10+` on

**How to apply:**
1. A suite verdict is the SUMMARY LINE, never an exit code. An output file with no pytest output
   means "did not run or was lost", whatever the code says.
2. Launch long suites detached with their own log (`nohup python -u -m pytest tests/ -q > log
   2>&1 &`, the `-u` matters or the log stays empty for minutes) and watch the log with a
   Monitor until-loop for the summary line.
3. Before relaunching anything DB-backed, list live python processes and match COMMAND LINES:
   two suites on one session database invalidate each other silently.
4. Distinguish your processes from other sessions' by command line before killing: this machine
   routinely runs parallel sessions with their own suites.

**How to apply:** before blaming a change for a hang, run
`Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='python.exe'"` and look for another `-m pytest`. It is
somebody else's session and must not be killed. Deselect the single contended node and get a verdict
on the rest, then run that node alone when the machine is quiet:

```bash
python -m pytest tests/ -q --timeout=600 --deselect "tests/test_legacy_document_extraction.py::test_libreoffice_converts_legacy_office_sources"
```

Measured: 5502 passed / 32 skipped with it deselected, then 4 passed running that file alone. Add
`--timeout` regardless, so a wedge becomes a traceback with a verdict instead of silence.

```text
[gw1] node down: Not properly terminated
... (gw0 through gw9, all ten)
1 skipped in 295.47s (0:04:55)
```

Exit code **0**. That is a genuine pytest summary line with a duration, so "does the file contain
a verdict" passes, and "is each answer a measurement or a default" passes too: `1 skipped` is a
measurement. It is simply a measurement of **one test out of 7,139**.

Two things worth separating:

the DATABASE for progress**, not the log, when checking on a run somebody else started: rows
  written are the only progress report that survives the session that started it.

🔑 The general shape: **a lock is only as safe as the thing that releases it.** A session-scoped
Postgres advisory lock is released by the backend dying and cannot get stuck. A file `flock` is held
by a process, and a process can be alive and unable to finish. Prefer the first where the choice
exists, and make sure the second cannot block on I/O nobody is reading.

Related: [[embedding-runs-on-vps2-one-at-a-time]], [[detached-runs-need-setsid]].

**Why:** the task wrapper hit its timeout and lost track of the child without killing it; exit 0
plus empty output is the same false-green signature the repo already documents for `claude -p`
([[claude-p-is-401-and-exits-zero]]). The suite here takes 30 to 55 minutes; any 10-minute cap
will produce this.

I reported a background indexing job as finished on the strength of an empty log and a failed
`kill -0 $(cat index_local.pid)`. It was still running, and had already written 3,891 chunks.

Both signals were worthless, for separate reasons:

- **Python buffers stdout when it is not a tty.** Under `nohup ... > log 2>&1` the log stays
  **0 bytes for the whole run** and appears at once at the end. recall's own `run_index.sh`
  already sets `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` and says why; I invoked the `.py` directly and lost it.
- **`kill -0 $(cat missing-file)`** fails identically to `kill -0 <dead-pid>`. A guard whose
  input is absent reports the same thing as a guard whose subject is gone, which is the
  [[guards-that-cannot-fail]] shape in a new place.

🔑 **The 2026-08-23 rule said an output file with no output means "did not run".** That was too
narrow. A file with plenty of output can still be a partial view, so the test is not "is the file
empty" but **"does the file contain a verdict for every unit I care about"**. Fifteen checks
existed; the file named two.

What I did instead, and what the answer must always come from, is the SERVICE rather than the
watcher:

```bash
gh pr checks <n> --json name,state -q '.[] | select(.state != "SUCCESS") | .name'
```

⚠️ **Corrected 2026-08-07. The previous version of this memory said ruff cannot launch here
(`os error 4551`, Application Control policy). That is no longer true and following it means
skipping a lint gate that works.**

Verified 2026-08-11, both forms launch:

- `python -m ruff check .` → **ruff 0.16.2**. Use this one. It now matches the repo's declared dev
  range, which #278 raised to `ruff>=0.16,<0.17` on 2026-08-11 (see [[recall-platform-floors]]).
- bare `ruff --version` → **ruff 0.6.9**, a much older install still on PATH.

**Why it matters:** RE-call's CI runs `ruff check .` as a hard gate in the `test` job, and it runs
**before pytest**, so the whole `test` job dies at lint and a green local pytest tells you nothing.
Two separate misses so far, both on files pyflakes called clean:

Empty output there, plus `gh run list --json status,conclusion` reading `completed / success`, is
the evidence. (Both said all 15 green on `c1436f7d`, so the exit code happened to be right, which
is precisely why this is worth writing down: a false green that agrees with the truth teaches
nothing unless you notice you never checked.)

⚠️ A pipeline's exit status is its LAST command's. Wrapping a watcher in `xargs` or a pipe means
the 0 you get back may not even be the watcher's own verdict.

## 🔁 Third instance, 2026-09-01: a progress probe on a detached run, and the file looked fine

🔑 **The 2026-09-01 rule was "does the file contain a verdict for every unit I care about".**
That is still too narrow, because here the file DID contain a line for every unit. The line was
`{}`. So the test has to be **"is each answer a measurement, or a default?"** An empty
collection, a zero count and a `None` are what a probe returns when it ran too early, and none of
them announces that. This is the same failure as
[[missing-input-becomes-a-clean-null]]: a default is indistinguishable from a real negative.

Two things that made the difference, and both are cheap:

The version was right and the command was still wrong: I ran `python -m ruff check` on **each file
as I wrote it** and never on the tree. CI runs `ruff check .` and failed with five findings, all in
one new test file, none of which the per-file runs had covered because I never pointed one at that
file.

⛔ **The argument to `ruff check` is part of the command. `python -m ruff check adapters/foo/` is
not a weaker version of the CI check, it is a different check.** Same failure family as the version
gap above and as [[windows-dev-linux-ci-hides-defects-in-both-directions]]: something that looked
like the CI command and was not.

Run the whole thing before pushing, which is also cheap:

```bash
python -m ruff check . && python -m pytest tests/ -q
```

Back to [MEMORY.md](MEMORY.md) and [feedback_index.md](feedback_index.md).

Waiting on a long remote job, I wrote this:

```bash
d=$(ssh host 'grep -c DONE log || echo 0')
if [ "$d" != "0" ]; then echo "finished"; break; fi
```

A timed-out `ssh` returns an **empty string**, and an empty string is not `"0"`, so **a failed check
read as a completed job**. I reported a batch as finished while it was 30% through, and only caught
it because the follow-up output was empty.

The same session produced the mirror image: a script that had DIED at 266 of 300 looked identical
to one still working, because I was watching a count and not a process. Half an hour of a paid run
was lost before anyone looked.

Same signature, third tool. A background probe on the `official-003` benchmark run notified
"completed (exit code 0)" with a **1,685-byte** output file that read as healthy: it printed a
records total, a corpus-doc line, an arms line, two full process command lines and three
`[ingest]` lines. Every section it promised was present.

It still answered nothing. `arms seen: {}` and `corpus doc counts: not recorded in records`,
because the probe's fixed `sleep 420` expired while the run was **mid-ingest**, before a single
record existed. The empty dict was not a finding, it was the absence of one, and it renders
identically to "the roster is broken".

And for liveness specifically, ask whether the PROCESS is alive, not whether a counter moved: a
finished job and a crashed job both stop moving. This is the same principle `CLAUDE.md` already
fixes for worktree claims, where "cannot tell" must count as ALIVE. The asymmetry is deliberate in
both directions: a false "still running" costs a wait, a false "done" costs a wrong result.

Two related traps from the same session, both cheap to avoid:

Measured 2026-08-20 in recall, at a cost of one 45-minute suite run killed at 43%.

`scripts/session-db.sh up` derives the container name from a hash of the checkout path, so the
container for `.claude/worktrees/agent-memory-recall-research-9ab019` was `recall-sess-0cd0d974`
whichever session started it. Another session claimed that worktree mid-run (see
[[sessionstart-hook-claims-workspaces]]), and its teardown removed *my* container while my `pytest`
was still using it.

## What the failure looks like, and why it misleads

**Why:** "still running" and "finished, wrote nothing" are the two readings of the same evidence,
and they call for opposite next actions, wait, or debug a failure that never happened.

**How to apply:** ask for the **process**, not its artefacts: `pgrep -f '<script>.py'`. Beware
that a `pgrep` pattern typed inside an `ssh`/`bash -c` command **matches that command itself**, so
exclude the wrapper or match the interpreter path. And run through the project's own wrapper
script when one exists, rather than the entry point it wraps.

A checkpoint mtime older than the per-item interval means dead, whatever the row count says.
`pgrep -af` run over SSH matches the SSH command line itself, which makes its output look like a
live process; filter it or check the mtime instead.

🔑 **Corollary worth the trouble**: per-item checkpointing paid for itself three times in one
session (a provider batch ceiling, an SSH reset, this HUP). Pair it with a fingerprint of the run's
settings on every row, so a resume under changed flags refuses instead of silently mixing two
configurations into one artifact.

Related: [[a-killed-shell-does-not-kill-the-work]], [[ci-runs-are-silently-not-created]].

**Why:** a workaround that relaxes a gate has no failure mode once the gate would have passed. It
does not error, it does not warn, it does not slow anything down. It just quietly downgrades every
answer from `trusted` to `degraded` and sets `calibrated=false`, and the only way to notice is to
go and ask whether the original condition still holds. Nobody does that, because the setting is
working — which is exactly what "working" looks like in both cases. A bug announces itself; a
stale exemption does not. This is the opposite polarity to a workaround that *breaks* when the
world moves, and it is far more durable for that reason.

⚠️ **Second, unrelated trap the same day: a background suite does not survive its session.** A
serial run launched in one session was killed at 54% by session teardown, and the
`SessionEnd` hook had already removed this checkout's DB container, so the log ended in large
consecutive blocks of `F` and `E`. **A cascade is diagnostic**: scattered failures are a code
problem, contiguous blocks are a shared resource that went away. A fresh container plus a rerun
inside one session was clean to 57% with zero failures.

Cost: about 90 minutes of wall clock across three non-runs, and zero wrong conclusions, because
CI was used as the authoritative gate instead (`7139 passed, 173 skipped`, twice).

This does **not** retire what follows. The port-1 default removes the *silent sharing* failure;
it does nothing about a quiet machine, foreign pytest processes, `tmp_path` pruning, or the
`::1` versus `0.0.0.0` split on 5432. Keep reading the skip count first.

## Before you run anything

**Start your own container.** There is no standing one to reuse. Through 2026-08-13 a
`recall-suite-db` sat on `127.0.0.1:55432` and this note said to reuse it; on 2026-08-14 the
container list had reached 26 leftovers and `docker container prune` removed all 25 stopped ones,
that among them. (Volumes survive a container prune, so 97 dangling volumes still hold the data,
but reattaching by hex id is not worth it.)

alpha015_items.text:
1. **Wait on the CONDITION, not the clock.** The replacement probe loops until `records >= 60`,
   re-checking that the process is alive each pass, so it cannot report a pre-ingest state as a
   state. A fixed sleep against a job whose phases have no fixed length is a coin flip.
2. **Alive is not working.** Having confirmed the process existed, I nearly stopped. `ps -o
   times` twice, 45 seconds apart, showed CPU climbing 156s (~350%, multi-threaded) and the HNSW
   `.bin` files growing: that is the evidence of progress. `pgrep` returning a pid is not.

1. **Is the process there at all?** `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='python.exe'"`
   with the command line printed. Match YOUR argv: on this machine there were **five concurrent
   pytest runs** from other sessions, so "a pytest is running" proves nothing about yours.
2. **Is it working or blocked?** Sample the CPU counter twice:
   `$p = Get-Process -Id <pid>; $p.CPU; Start-Sleep 20; $p.Refresh(); $p.CPU`. Mine went 995s to
   1002s in 20 wall seconds: alive, and starved to a third of a core by the other four suites.
3. Only then consider the output file.

**How to apply:** never end a backgrounded run with `| tail`. Write the full output and read the
tail of the FILE, or use `tee`. Reserve `tail` for foreground commands whose output you want
trimmed. And before restarting anything long, check liveness by process and CPU, because a restart
under contention costs the whole elapsed run and lands in the same queue.

**`RECALL_OIDC_SUBJECT_TENANTS` CONSTRAINS the tenant claim, it does not SUPPLY it.** I assumed it
let the deployment name the tenant and skip the claim. It does not: the token must still carry
`tenant`, and the binding then refuses a subject not bound to it. That is the configuration to
prefer over `RECALL_OIDC_TRUST_TENANT_CLAIM` (the IdP asserts, the deployment constrains), but it
means the IdP must emit the claim — and on Keycloak 24+ that additionally needs **unmanaged
attributes enabled on the realm's user profile**, or the attribute is silently dropped and the
token carries `tenant: null`.

query.query: An old workspace claim says its PID is alive. What identity check must come before forcing release?

pool.text:
🔑 **So the three checks are not independent votes, they are ordered.** The process NAME is the
decisive one; the branch check only becomes evidence once the pid is known not to be a live
`claude.exe`. Read the other way round it argues for `release --force` against a session that is
mid-edit, which is the exact failure the "cannot tell counts as alive" asymmetry exists to
prevent.

Corrected order, cheapest decisive first:

1. `Get-Process -Id <pid>` and read **ProcessName**. `claude` -> the claim is live, STOP, do not
   force. Anything else (`svchost`, ...) -> recycled pid, continue.
2. Only then, the branch comparison and the age, to decide whether forcing is right.

`_process_alive` in `scripts/session-space.sh` asks `tasklist //FI "PID eq $pid"` and treats any
match as alive, which is deliberate and documented: "cannot tell" counts as alive, because a false
alive costs a `release --force` while a false dead costs somebody's in-flight work. That asymmetry
is right. The consequence is that **a recycled pid makes a claim immortal**: `_claim_is_stale`
returns early on the liveness check and never reaches the age comparison, so the worktree can never
be taken over by the rule that exists for exactly this case.

**How to apply it.** Before believing a live pid on a claim older than `STALE_HOURS`, check the
process NAME, not merely its existence. Three signals settled it here in under a minute, and the
third is the one no pid table can fake:

```bash
tasklist //FI "PID eq $(sed -n 's/^pid=//p' <worktree>/.git/claude-session-claim)" //NH
tasklist //FI "IMAGENAME eq claude.exe" //NH        # is that pid among them at all?
git -C <worktree> rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD       # vs the `branch=` the claim recorded
```

The branch check is the cheap decisive one: this claim named
`claude/mempalace-benchmark-investigation-ae9fdb` while the worktree sat on
`claude/embedding-cache-recall-f0f439`, so whatever wrote the claim was not what last used the
directory. With a clean tree and no `claude.exe` at that pid, `release --force` was correct rather
than merely convenient.

```text
pid 6276 -> ProcessName: claude, StartTime 01/09/2026 21:14:49   (a real session, 2.5h old)
claim says:  fix/560-trust-refusal-reaches-the-client
actual HEAD: feat/recall-inventory
```

Both true at once. A session that checks out a different branch AFTER claiming produces exactly
the signature this memo reads as "whatever wrote the claim was not what last used the directory",
because the claim records the branch **at claim time** and nothing rewrites it.

A staleness test made of "is the holder alive?" and "is the record old?" gives opposite answers
depending on which runs first, and only one order is safe.

The bug, in both `scripts/session-space.sh` and the first draft of `scripts/session_start_hook.py`:

```python
when = claim.get("claimed_epoch", "")
if not when.isdigit():
    return True          # "an unreadable claim is stale"
if process_alive(claim.get("pid", "")):
    return False
```

A claim whose timestamp is **missing or truncated** was declared stale **without the liveness check
ever running**, so a worktree held by a running process was taken over. Reproduced against a live
`claude.exe`, 2026-08-16. A torn concurrent write produces precisely that file, so the two bugs feed
each other: see [[noclobber-is-not-atomic-on-msys]].

Measured 2026-08-30 opening a session in `.claude/worktrees/funny-neumann-344dd0`. The workspace
was REFUSED: claim held by session `ac1646af`, `pid: 7468 (alive)`, claimed 26 hours earlier
against a 12 hour `STALE_HOURS`.

The pid was alive and it was **`svchost`**. Windows had recycled 7468 to an unrelated system
process after the claiming `claude.exe` exited.

🔑 **The rule already existed in this project and I was applying it in another file the same day.**
recall's `CLAUDE.md` says of workspace claims: liveness is asked of the OS rather than assumed, and
*"cannot tell" counts as alive: a false alive costs a `release --force`, a false dead costs
somebody's in-flight work.* I knew it as a rule about CLAIM FILES and did not carry it into a watch
I wrote an hour later. A rule filed under the case that taught it does not transfer itself.

## How to apply

A test can pass because of something in your environment that will not be in
anyone else's, and nothing about the green result says so.

`scripts/session-space.sh` recorded `SESSION_PID="${CLAUDE_PID:-$$}"`. Inside a
Claude session `CLAUDE_PID` is a real Windows pid that `tasklist` can see. Outside
one, which is both the documented manual workflow and **every CI runner**, `$$`
is an MSYS pid that tasklist cannot see, so `_process_alive` judged every claim
lock holder DEAD and each racer broke the others' locks. Mutual exclusion did not
degrade; it stopped existing.

**Measured:** four concurrent claims, **two winners** on a clean Windows runner.
Green here for weeks. Reproduced locally the instant I ran the same suite with
`env -u CLAUDE_PID`.

- [A claim pid can be recycled into a live stranger](a-claim-pid-can-be-recycled-into-a-live-stranger.md) — a 26h-old claim read `alive` because pid 7468 had become `svchost`; a recycled pid makes a claim immortal, so check the process NAME and the claim's `branch=` before believing it.

⚠️ Existence alone is what fools you, and both PowerShell's `Get-Process -Id` and the script's
`tasklist //FI "PID eq ..."` answer existence, not identity. I used `Get-Process -Id` here to
decide whether another session's containers were mine to remove, got the right answer, and had
verified nothing: the recycled-pid case would have returned the same "alive".

Cost: nothing, because the containers were left alone either way. The decision it was feeding
(remove another session's 5 running containers) is one where a false "dead" destroys live work.

Cost: nothing this time, because the checks are seconds. The cost of NOT knowing it is a worktree
that no session may ever open again, which reads as a mysterious permanent refusal.

Related: [[a-claim-can-be-dead-while-the-checkout-is-live]] is the same file failing the other way
round, a claim gone stale under a session that kept working. Between them: a claim file is evidence
about the past, never about the present.

## ⚠️ 2026-09-01: the branch check is NOT decisive on its own, and treating it so risks the harm

Applying this memo to `server-launch-verification-gap-702149` produced a **branch mismatch on a
genuinely live session**, which is the combination the "cheap decisive" framing above does not
allow for.

- `git fetch` and check `HEAD..origin/master` **before** pushing any branch older than a day, and
  read what those commits did rather than only counting them. A commit titled "take X out of the
  tree" on a branch you do not have is a signal to rebase before pushing, not after.
- After rebasing onto a security fix, run the repo's own guard test specifically. It is the only
  thing that knows what was removed.
- ⛔ **A force-push does not unpublish.** GitHub serves the old SHA until it garbage-collects, and
  pull-request refs keep old commits alive indefinitely. Say that plainly instead of claiming the
  content is gone. See [[a-force-push-does-not-unpublish-a-file-on-github]].

**And a lock must be reclaimable**, or it is a worse failure than the race. The
first version could not be: a holder killed without running its trap blocked
every future claim forever, `release --force` did not clear it, and `whose`
reported "unclaimed" at the same time. Record the holder's pid, break a
demonstrably dead holder's lock, keep "cannot tell" meaning alive, and make the
documented recovery actually recover.

**How to apply:** when fixing a race, enumerate every writer of the resource, not
just the one in the bug report. Ask of each: is this a create, or a
read-modify-write? Only the first is fixable without a lock.

Related: [[guards-that-cannot-fail]], [[noclobber-is-not-atomic-on-msys]],
[[liveness-before-timestamp]], [[audit-after-merge-is-too-late]].

Measured 2026-08-20 while deciding which containers were safe to stop.
`.claude/worktrees/prereg-successor` carried a claim naming **pid 19900, dead**, timestamped
**24 hours earlier**, which is past the 12 hour `STALE_HOURS` threshold. By
`scripts/session-space.sh` that worktree was takeable. It was not: a git checkout had run there
**14 minutes** before, and its containers had been started 3 and 7 hours earlier, long after the
claim was written.

So the claim had gone stale **under a session that kept working**, presumably one that resumed
under a new pid without re-claiming. The staleness rule is sound for the failure it was built for,
an abandoned worktree, and it is silent about this one.

The standing instruction says: never edit a number in a committed pre-registration, and *"a gate
must never be able to force this edit. If a check demands a change to a pre-registration, the check
is wrong and gets an exemption, not the record."*

The safe graph RAG release claim is trust and serving hardening. `graph_expansion=one_hop` walks
the deterministic semantic graph, not the separate authored supersession reasoning graph. It
checks readiness, trusted seeds, generation identity, and the selective gate before projection;
whole expansion refusals are separate from discovered candidate rejections; and every admitted
candidate passes ordinary trust evaluation again. The post release range contains no new positive
retrieval quality measurement, so the release must not claim higher recall. Re-measure the baseline
with the commands above before revising this scope.

  not symmetric, so the tie goes to alive.

**Before acting on a stale claim, check the worktree's own activity**, which no claim file can fake:

```bash
find <worktree> -type f -not -path '*/.git/*' -not -path '*mypy_cache*' -not -name '*.pyc' -printf '%TY-%Tm-%TdT%TH:%TM %p\n' | sort -r | head -5
```

guard has a cheap check and an expensive one, and the cheap one is written first out of habit. If
the cheap check can return a *verdict* rather than a *hint*, the expensive one is dead code on
exactly the inputs that need it most.

**How to apply:**

- **Two classes of check.** Instruction parity is an INVARIANT, always enforced: a roster whose
  arms do not share one protocol byte for byte is not measuring what it claims, whatever the run
  is for. The corpus floor is an EXPECTATION, enforced only when supplied, because
  `diagnostic-010` ran 125 sessions deliberately. Conflating the two would either break pilots or
  let official runs through.
- **A SKIP is never a PASS.** An absent field reports SKIP and the summary says so in words. A
  check that could not run and a check that passed rendering identically is the precise failure
  the whole script exists to answer, so it must not reproduce it.

- **A test must not inherit what it is testing.** The racers now run under
  `env -u CLAUDE_PID` so the hard path is the only path they can take.
- **Ask what is in your environment that a runner will not have.** An exported
  variable, a running process, a container, a cached credential. Each one is a
  way for a test to pass for the wrong reason.

  the first run was luck. Five rounds took it to 3 of 3 red on the mutant and

## Two adjacent traps, same family

**How to apply:** never trust the `--check` narration alone. Ask the kernel who holds the fd, which
answers regardless of the process name:

```bash
ssh vps2 'fuser -v ~/recall-repos/.locks/embed.lock; lsof ~/recall-repos/.locks/embed.lock'
```

A held flock **cannot** be stale: the kernel drops it however the process dies. So if `fuser`
names a live pid, there is a real run and the answer is to wait, never to force. If `fuser` names
nothing, the lock is already free and the refusal would not have happened.

**Fix worth making:** widen the probe beyond `index_memory` (or drop the probe and report `fuser`
output directly), and stop printing "nothing running" when the lock is held. Not done here.

Cost: no damage, because the guard held. The near-miss was the diagnosis, not the lock.

🔑 **So the three checks are not independent votes, they are ordered.** The process NAME is the
decisive one; the branch check only becomes evidence once the pid is known not to be a live
`claude.exe`. Read the other way round it argues for `release --force` against a session that is
mid-edit, which is the exact failure the "cannot tell counts as alive" asymmetry exists to
prevent.

Corrected order, cheapest decisive first:

1. `Get-Process -Id <pid>` and read **ProcessName**. `claude` -> the claim is live, STOP, do not
   force. Anything else (`svchost`, ...) -> recycled pid, continue.
2. Only then, the branch comparison and the age, to decide whether forcing is right.

`_process_alive` in `scripts/session-space.sh` asks `tasklist //FI "PID eq $pid"` and treats any
match as alive, which is deliberate and documented: "cannot tell" counts as alive, because a false
alive costs a `release --force` while a false dead costs somebody's in-flight work. That asymmetry
is right. The consequence is that **a recycled pid makes a claim immortal**: `_claim_is_stale`
returns early on the liveness check and never reaches the age comparison, so the worktree can never
be taken over by the rule that exists for exactly this case.

**How to apply it.** Before believing a live pid on a claim older than `STALE_HOURS`, check the
process NAME, not merely its existence. Three signals settled it here in under a minute, and the
third is the one no pid table can fake:

```bash
tasklist //FI "PID eq $(sed -n 's/^pid=//p' <worktree>/.git/claude-session-claim)" //NH
tasklist //FI "IMAGENAME eq claude.exe" //NH        # is that pid among them at all?
git -C <worktree> rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD       # vs the `branch=` the claim recorded
```

The branch check is the cheap decisive one: this claim named
`claude/mempalace-benchmark-investigation-ae9fdb` while the worktree sat on
`claude/embedding-cache-recall-f0f439`, so whatever wrote the claim was not what last used the
directory. With a clean tree and no `claude.exe` at that pid, `release --force` was correct rather
than merely convenient.

```text
pid 6276 -> ProcessName: claude, StartTime 01/09/2026 21:14:49   (a real session, 2.5h old)
claim says:  fix/560-trust-refusal-reaches-the-client
actual HEAD: feat/recall-inventory
```

Both true at once. A session that checks out a different branch AFTER claiming produces exactly
the signature this memo reads as "whatever wrote the claim was not what last used the directory",
because the claim records the branch **at claim time** and nothing rewrites it.

A staleness test made of "is the holder alive?" and "is the record old?" gives opposite answers
depending on which runs first, and only one order is safe.

The bug, in both `scripts/session-space.sh` and the first draft of `scripts/session_start_hook.py`:

```python
when = claim.get("claimed_epoch", "")
if not when.isdigit():
    return True          # "an unreadable claim is stale"
if process_alive(claim.get("pid", "")):
    return False
```

ever running**, so a worktree held by a running process was taken over. Reproduced against a live
`claude.exe`, 2026-08-16. A torn concurrent write produces precisely that file, so the two bugs feed
each other: see [[noclobber-is-not-atomic-on-msys]].

**How to apply:** when a guard scans files, ask what fraction of the tracked tree it can actually
read, and check the answer against the file types the project publishes. Then write the test as a
**positive control**: build an artifact whose raw bytes do NOT contain the needle, assert that,
and assert the scanner finds it anyway. Asserting only that the real tree is clean cannot
distinguish a scanner that reads the file from one that skips it, which is exactly how this
survived. Decide explicitly what a file that will not decompress does: here it falls back to the
raw bytes, so a corrupt archive cannot become a hiding place.

⛔ **So "does the injected context reach the agent" cannot be measured from the transcript**, and
the obvious way to measure it returns the wrong answer with no error. I was one grep away from
recording a working mechanism as a plumbing failure and ending the lane on it.

🔑 The general shape, which has now cost this project twice: **absence in a log is evidence only
once you have shown the log records that kind of event at all.** The same reasoning had just
produced a clean bill of health for a CLAUDE.md leak check that grepped the same streams, and that
one was also worthless. The fix in both cases is a **positive control**: inject a nonce, then
confirm you can see the nonce, before trusting any absence in the same instrument.

🔑 **The failure is silent about its cause.** The message names `eval()` and says nothing about the
text that actually matched, so the obvious reading is that the hook found a real `eval()` call. It
did not.

🔑 **Retrying the identical call succeeds.** The block is per-invocation, not sticky, so the repair
is to reissue the same Write/Edit rather than to rewrite the code around the hook. Do NOT rename an
identifier to appease it: that would let a scanner accident dictate a public API name.

🔑 **It fired on the memo describing it.** Writing this file was itself refused once, then accepted
on retry, which is a positive control most tooling notes never get.

**Why:** a detector that reads as coverage is worse than no detector, because it stops anyone looking
again. The docstring is what made the gap survive: it described a design nobody had built, and this
audit nearly accepted it on the strength of the comment alone.

**How to apply:** when auditing any instrument, do not stop at "it fired". Follow one finding to
where it is supposed to land and confirm it is there. Read the sink, not the docstring. Then mutate
the detector so it *should* fire and confirm the row appears, and give it an input it should ignore
and confirm nothing appears. Fixed here by appending JSON rows to
`~/.claude/governance-events.log`; verified live, with a real Bash call in this session producing a
row carrying that session's own id.

**How to apply:** before trusting a kill rate, enumerate the ways the system under test can reach
the state you are asserting about, from the *source of that state*, not from your own test file. If
a claim is a universal ("a degraded result always..."), find the branch that produces it and check
your fixture actually contains each one. Write the test from the shape that would **violate** the
claim; if you cannot construct one, say why in the test rather than assuming none exists. Same
family as the balanced fixture that cannot discriminate

1. **Before believing a negative, ask what a positive would look like on this apparatus, and go

   negative either.
2. **A filtered test run is not a test run.** State the filter next to the count, always: "1,299

## The rule set is small on purpose, and that is the whole design

It screens prose **about** engineering, which is the worst input for a naive scanner: the corpus
legitimately holds example DSNs, host names, git shas and paragraphs discussing credentials, and
recall's own `CLAUDE.md` contains `postgresql://user:pw@localhost/recall`. **A screen that fires on
those is not cautious, it is ignored.** Every rule is anchored on a vendor prefix plus a length, or
a PEM header. Bare high-entropy strings, database URLs and proximity to the word "password" are
deliberately not screened, and the module says so: a secret with no distinctive shape gets through.

the effective value after a systemd change, never trust the file. Known instances:
- ✅ `updown-book-1hz.service` — wanted `=0` (never give up; feeds the LIVE racers), got
  10s/5. **FIXED + deployed, PR #1892** (effective `10s` → `0`, PID preserved). Was LATENT:
  `RestartSec=10` kept starts under 5-per-10s ⇒ **correct only by accident** — lowering
  RestartSec would have made it silently give up.
- ✅ `polymarket-sales-bot.service` + `polymarket-stripe-webhook.service` — **were broken in
  GIT ONLY; the live VPS2 box was already CORRECT**

**How to apply:** when a guard scans files, ask what fraction of the tracked tree it can actually
read, and check the answer against the file types the project publishes. Then write the test as a
**positive control**: build an artifact whose raw bytes do NOT contain the needle, assert that,
and assert the scanner finds it anyway. Asserting only that the real tree is clean cannot
distinguish a scanner that reads the file from one that skips it, which is exactly how this
survived. Decide explicitly what a file that will not decompress does: here it falls back to the
raw bytes, so a corrupt archive cannot become a hiding place.

⛔ **So "does the injected context reach the agent" cannot be measured from the transcript**, and
the obvious way to measure it returns the wrong answer with no error. I was one grep away from
recording a working mechanism as a plumbing failure and ending the lane on it.

🔑 The general shape, which has now cost this project twice: **absence in a log is evidence only
once you have shown the log records that kind of event at all.** The same reasoning had just
produced a clean bill of health for a CLAUDE.md leak check that grepped the same streams, and that
one was also worthless. The fix in both cases is a **positive control**: inject a nonce, then
confirm you can see the nonce, before trusting any absence in the same instrument.

**Why:** a detector that reads as coverage is worse than no detector, because it stops anyone looking
again. The docstring is what made the gap survive: it described a design nobody had built, and this
audit nearly accepted it on the strength of the comment alone.

**How to apply:** when auditing any instrument, do not stop at "it fired". Follow one finding to
where it is supposed to land and confirm it is there. Read the sink, not the docstring. Then mutate
the detector so it *should* fire and confirm the row appears, and give it an input it should ignore
and confirm nothing appears. Fixed here by appending JSON rows to
`~/.claude/governance-events.log`; verified live, with a real Bash call in this session producing a
row carrying that session's own id.

That fix existed **only** as a deployed file. `git log --all -S SELFTEST_MATCH -- scripts/test_receipt.py`
was empty and the only other copy on disk was the same stale 10017 bytes, so one obedient `cp`
would have erased it leaving no diff, no branch and no record that anything was lost.

**Why:** a drift check knows the two copies differ. It does **not** know which one is right, and
the remedy it prints has to guess. It guesses "the repository is canonical" because that is true
almost always, and the exception is exactly the interesting case: an artefact fixed in place,
under time pressure, by whoever was debugging the thing it guards.

**How to apply:** when any "deployed matches source" check fails, **establish the direction of the
drift before following the printed remedy**. `diff` the two, compare mtimes and sizes, and ask
version control whether the newer content exists anywhere (`git log --all -S <distinctive-token>`).
If the deployed side is newer, the fix is to adopt it into the repository, not to overwrite it. An
improvement that lives only as a deployed artefact is one redeploy away from being erased, so
rescuing it is worth more than the failing test that revealed it.

This generalises past hooks: the same asymmetry applies to a config file edited live on a server, a
crontab, a systemd unit, and any dashboard definition maintained through a UI.

**How to apply:**
- On VPS3, default to **read-only** (`ssh vps3 "cat ..."`, `journalctl`, `systemctl is-active`, vps3-lite read). No writes, no `systemctl restart`, no deploy/rsync, no env edits — only with explicit per-action approval (and on VPS3 the agent never applies env/restart anyway; provide root the copy-from-`_cf_deploy` commands).
- Reconciliation direction is **VPS3 → git** (capture live drift INTO the repo), **never git → VPS3** over the hotfixes. Before any `master→VPS3` deploy of a drifted file, reconcile VPS3's version into git first or the deploy regresses live trading.
- When resolving merges/PRs that touch live subsystems, verify against the actual VPS3 deployment and treat VPS3 as canonical; scope/align so the change never regresses what's running.

baseline_items.text:
That fix existed **only** as a deployed file. `git log --all -S SELFTEST_MATCH -- scripts/test_receipt.py`
was empty and the only other copy on disk was the same stale 10017 bytes, so one obedient `cp`
would have erased it leaving no diff, no branch and no record that anything was lost.

**Why:** a drift check knows the two copies differ. It does **not** know which one is right, and
the remedy it prints has to guess. It guesses "the repository is canonical" because that is true
almost always, and the exception is exactly the interesting case: an artefact fixed in place,
under time pressure, by whoever was debugging the thing it guards.

**How to apply:** when any "deployed matches source" check fails, **establish the direction of the
drift before following the printed remedy**. `diff` the two, compare mtimes and sizes, and ask
version control whether the newer content exists anywhere (`git log --all -S <distinctive-token>`).
If the deployed side is newer, the fix is to adopt it into the repository, not to overwrite it. An
improvement that lives only as a deployed artefact is one redeploy away from being erased, so
rescuing it is worth more than the failing test that revealed it.

This generalises past hooks: the same asymmetry applies to a config file edited live on a server, a
crontab, a systemd unit, and any dashboard definition maintained through a UI.

**How to apply:**
- On VPS3, default to **read-only** (`ssh vps3 "cat ..."`, `journalctl`, `systemctl is-active`, vps3-lite read). No writes, no `systemctl restart`, no deploy/rsync, no env edits — only with explicit per-action approval (and on VPS3 the agent never applies env/restart anyway; provide root the copy-from-`_cf_deploy` commands).
- Reconciliation direction is **VPS3 → git** (capture live drift INTO the repo), **never git → VPS3** over the hotfixes. Before any `master→VPS3` deploy of a drifted file, reconcile VPS3's version into git first or the deploy regresses live trading.
- When resolving merges/PRs that touch live subsystems, verify against the actual VPS3 deployment and treat VPS3 as canonical; scope/align so the change never regresses what's running.
- The auto-mode

query.query: A cache module and its tests already exist. How can I verify that production really uses it?

pool.text:
**Why this is not an accident.** Nothing fails when a facility has no callers. Tests pass, because
they call it directly. Coverage is fine, for the same reason. The docstring said "Opt-in: nothing
uses it unless a cache is explicitly passed", which is true, accurate, and reads as a design
decision rather than as a gap. Only a caller census tells the two apart.

**How to apply it.** Before building something that sounds like it should already exist, run three
greps, in this order, and read the third as the real answer:

```bash
grep -rln "<concept>" recall/ --include=*.py          # does it exist
grep -rn "def <entry_point>" recall/ --include=*.py   # what is its entry point
grep -rn "<entry_point>(" --include=*.py . | grep -v tests/ | grep -v benchmarks/   # who CALLS it
```

2026-08-30. Asked to add a content-addressed embedding cache to recall, I found one already in
`recall/cache.py`: keyed on the full `EmbeddingProfile.fingerprint` plus the encoder purpose, which
is a stronger key than the `sha256(text) + model + dim` being proposed, with `tests/test_cache.py`
and `tests/test_embedding_cache_identity.py` behind it.

**It was reaching nothing.** `grep -rn "cache=" ` over `Indexer(` constructions returned ONE caller
in the whole repository, `benchmarks/ladder/systems/recall_system.py`. `GenerationManager.build`,
the route production actually takes, called `embed_passages` directly. So the feature existed, was
correct, was tested, and no user-facing run had ever used it.

An empty third result is the finding. It converts "build a cache" into "wire the cache", which is a
smaller, safer change and keeps the stronger key somebody already thought about.

One trap met while wiring it: `recall/setup.py::index_memory_directory` catches `Exception` and
prints a friendly message, so passing a new kwarg its test's fake `Indexer` did not accept turned a
failing test into a **silently skipped** one (`KeyError: 'path'` on an assertion that never ran).
Best-effort error handling makes wiring mistakes invisible; assert the wiring explicitly there.

Related: [[a-check-that-cannot-fail-looks-like-a-pass]], [[a-workaround-outlives-the-problem-silently]].

# Consensus selection-copy — shadow module BUILT (not deployed) 2026-06-21

Reframe of copytrade's binding constraint (**too few individually-reliable wallets**): stop
depending on single-wallet reliability — copy the **quality-weighted convergence** of a panel on a
market *selection*. Latency-insensitive (copies which market to be in, not entry timing) → hold-to-settle.
The right tools already existed in-repo (`wallet_skill_permutation.py` LBS/Yale skill test; block-bootstrap
CI; `scripts/psw_market_signals.py` consensus aggregator) — but psw was DORMANT + had a broken live-insert
(stale schema) + used an opaque external panel. This module fixes all three. Builds on
[[project_sports_lrp_wallet_scan_2026-06-20]], [[project_curated_top_cooccurrence_hunt_2026-06-16]].

```bash
grep -rn "<ENV_VAR_THE_DOCS_NAME>" --include=*.py . | grep -v tests/
```

An empty result against a variable the docs present as configuration is the same finding as an
empty caller list, and it is the more alarming one, because somebody wrote a sentence claiming
otherwise.

Two further traps met here, both worth the sentence:

> ✅ **FIXED SAME DAY by #1993.** The economics were never missing — `recorder.report_rows_from_events`
> was pure and unit-tested, with **no production caller**, because the design defers economics to
> gate time on purpose. `shadow/gate_report.py` is that caller and computes C1–C4 **offline from
> already-recorded rows**, so C2/C3 are obtainable on the existing 3 fills without new data.
> 🔑 The sharper lesson: **the feature existed and the CALLER did not** — "unbuilt" was the wrong
> diagnosis. A pure, well-tested function with no caller is indistinguishable from a missing
> feature when you only look at its output column.

**What is new, and what makes this the harder version.** The cache's docstring said "Opt-in:
nothing uses it unless a cache is explicitly passed", which is honest and merely reads as a design
decision. Here `docs/REASONING_API.md` said *"The MCP server can provide a local Ollama adapter"*
and named `RECALL_REASONING_ANSWER_PROVIDER=ollama` as the selector. **That variable was read
nowhere in the tree.** So the documentation actively asserted the wiring existed, and a reader
doing the honest thing (read the docs before grepping) is led away from the census.

🔑 **Documentation is not a caller census, and a doc that describes a wiring is evidence about
somebody's intent, not about the code.** Add a fourth grep, and let it beat the prose:

# Decision

The graph has now shown a repeatable retrieval benefit on LoCoMo, but the useful mechanism is much
narrower than generic graph expansion. It acts as a structural reranker inside the ordinary top 20:
protect the first eight direct results, find graph linked items among the remaining candidates, rank
them with their existing retrieval scores, and let at most two compete for the last two positions in
a fixed ten item context. The current production graph path excludes every raw top 20 result from
graph admission, so it cannot execute the mechanism that produced the positive benchmark result.

Future work should start by closing this production parity gap. Do not start with wider traversal,
more graph slots, additional cache work, or an unrestricted multi hop method.

# Generation graph metadata cache follow-up

Measured and implemented on 2026-09-12 in the RE-call worktree.

## Finding

The post PR 631 live attribution showed graph one hop still paid 17 database statements and 445180
bytes at p50, with a p95 of 455355 bytes, while graph off paid 7 statements and 149016 bytes at
p50. The warm projection and adjacency caches were already effective. The remaining repeated graph
cost was the `GenerationStore.supersession_all` generation scan, which bypassed the legacy store's
cache and transferred its full result for every graph request. `GenerationStore.graph_readiness`
also reread the compact positive marker for every request.

## Change

🔑 **This is the same shape as [[a-facility-can-be-complete-tested-and-unreached]] in recall's
store**, where the embedding cache had three test files and exactly one caller. A capability that
is built, shipped, allowed and never invoked is indistinguishable in every metric from one that
does not exist.

`contradictory` (-10, p=0.021) needs the agent to notice that two retrieved documents disagree.
That is plausibly what a reasoning or audit tool is for. **Before building conflict detection,
find out whether recall already has it and the agent just never asks.** The cheap probe: replay a
handful of `contradictory` cells with the reasoning tools called explicitly, and see whether the
outcome changes.

**Why this is not an accident.** Nothing fails when a facility has no callers. Tests pass, because
they call it directly. Coverage is fine, for the same reason. The docstring said "Opt-in: nothing
uses it unless a cache is explicitly passed", which is true, accurate, and reads as a design
decision rather than as a gap. Only a caller census tells the two apart.

**How to apply it.** Before building something that sounds like it should already exist, run three
greps, in this order, and read the third as the real answer:

```bash
grep -rln "<concept>" recall/ --include=*.py          # does it exist
grep -rn "def <entry_point>" recall/ --include=*.py   # what is its entry point
grep -rn "<entry_point>(" --include=*.py . | grep -v tests/ | grep -v benchmarks/   # who CALLS it
```

2026-08-30. Asked to add a content-addressed embedding cache to recall, I found one already in
`recall/cache.py`: keyed on the full `EmbeddingProfile.fingerprint` plus the encoder purpose, which
is a stronger key than the `sha256(text) + model + dim` being proposed, with `tests/test_cache.py`
and `tests/test_embedding_cache_identity.py` behind it.

**It was reaching nothing.** `grep -rn "cache=" ` over `Indexer(` constructions returned ONE caller
in the whole repository, `benchmarks/ladder/systems/recall_system.py`. `GenerationManager.build`,
the route production actually takes, called `embed_passages` directly. So the feature existed, was
correct, was tested, and no user-facing run had ever used it.

An empty third result is the finding. It converts "build a cache" into "wire the cache", which is a
smaller, safer change and keeps the stronger key somebody already thought about.

One trap met while wiring it: `recall/setup.py::index_memory_directory` catches `Exception` and
prints a friendly message, so passing a new kwarg its test's fake `Indexer` did not accept turned a
failing test into a **silently skipped** one (`KeyError: 'path'` on an assertion that never ran).
Best-effort error handling makes wiring mistakes invisible; assert the wiring explicitly there.

Related: [[a-check-that-cannot-fail-looks-like-a-pass]], [[a-workaround-outlives-the-problem-silently]].

Waiting on a long remote job, I wrote this:

```bash

if [ "$d" != "0" ]; then echo "finished"; break; fi
```

A timed-out `ssh` returns an **empty string**, and an empty string is not `"0"`, so **a failed check
read as a completed job**. I reported a batch as finished while it was 30% through, and only caught
it because the follow-up output was empty.

The same session produced the mirror image: a script that had DIED at 266 of 300 looked identical
to one still working, because I was watching a count and not a process. Half an hour of a paid run
was lost before anyone looked.

A checkpoint mtime older than the per-item interval means dead, whatever the row count says.
`pgrep -af` run over SSH matches the SSH command line itself, which makes its output look like a
live process; filter it or check the mtime instead.

session (a provider batch ceiling, an SSH reset, this HUP). Pair it with a fingerprint of the run's
settings on every row, so a resume under changed flags refuses instead of silently mixing two
configurations into one artifact.

Related: [[a-killed-shell-does-not-kill-the-work]], [[ci-runs-are-silently-not-created]].

when the SSH session closed. The wrapper was backgrounded but stayed in the session's process

been frozen for 39 minutes.

**A probe that fails to answer has told you nothing. It has NOT told you the thing is gone.**

I armed a monitor over a queued run on VPS2. Its liveness check was:

```bash
alive=$(ssh -o BatchMode=yes vps2 "pgrep -f '...'" 2>/dev/null || true)
if [ -z "$alive" ]; then echo "QUEUE PROCESS IS GONE"; break; fi
```

It fired within minutes. The process was **alive**, pid 635206, and its log showed it had been
ticking every ten minutes for an hour afterwards. The `|| true` and the `2>/dev/null` collapsed
three different outcomes into one empty string: *the process is gone*, *ssh failed*, and *the host
is loaded and slow*. The host was at load 24 with sixteen sessions at the time, so a transient was
the most likely of the three and got reported as the most alarming.

  run. It now requires the probe to echo a sentinel and refuses on anything else. See
  [[git-bash-fork-failures-kill-scripts-silently]] for why 127 is common here.

  negative age is true, so an NTP step or a restored state file suppressed every tick forever
  while the task reported success. Unusable data must make the run eligible, never eternally
  ineligible.

  a loss that never happened.

The bug, in both `scripts/session-space.sh` and the first draft of `scripts/session_start_hook.py`:


A claim whose timestamp is **missing or truncated** was declared stale **without the liveness check
ever running**, so a worktree held by a running process was taken over. Reproduced against a live
`claude.exe`, 2026-08-16. A torn concurrent write produces precisely that file, so the two bugs feed
each other: see [[noclobber-is-not-atomic-on-msys]].


other diagnostic that mentions the same string.

Back to [MEMORY.md](MEMORY.md) and [feedback_index.md](feedback_index.md).

**A probe that fails to answer has told you nothing. It has NOT told you the thing is gone.**

I armed a monitor over a queued run on VPS2. Its liveness check was:

```bash
alive=$(ssh -o BatchMode=yes vps2 "pgrep -f '...'" 2>/dev/null || true)
if [ -z "$alive" ]; then echo "QUEUE PROCESS IS GONE"; break; fi
```

It fired within minutes. The process was **alive**, pid 635206, and its log showed it had been
ticking every ten minutes for an hour afterwards. The `|| true` and the `2>/dev/null` collapsed
three different outcomes into one empty string: *the process is gone*, *ssh failed*, and *the host
is loaded and slow*. The host was at load 24 with sixteen sessions at the time, so a transient was
the most likely of the three and got reported as the most alarming.

* **Keep the probe's exit code.** `|| true` and `2>/dev/null` are how "unreachable" becomes
  indistinguishable from "absent". Capture `$?` and branch on it before reading the output.
* **Require CONSECUTIVE negative observations from SUCCESSFUL probes** before declaring death.
  Three is enough to clear a network blip; one is never enough.
* **Report an unreachable host as unreachable.** It is a real event worth a message, and it is a
  different message from "your run died".
* ⚠️ **Bias a watch the safe way round.** A false "still running" costs one more check later. A
  false "it died" costs a relaunch, a duplicate run against a shared corpus, or a person acting on
  a loss that never happened.

And for liveness specifically, ask whether the PROCESS is alive, not whether a counter moved: a
finished job and a crashed job both stop moving. This is the same principle `CLAUDE.md` already
fixes for worktree claims, where "cannot tell" must count as ALIVE. The asymmetry is deliberate in
both directions: a false "still running" costs a wait, a false "done" costs a wrong result.

Two related traps from the same session, both cheap to avoid:

A long run on VPS2 launched as `nohup bash script.sh > log 2>&1 &` died silently at row 29 of 500
when the SSH session closed. The wrapper was backgrounded but stayed in the session's process
group, so it took the HUP. Relaunched with `setsid nohup ... < /dev/null &` it ran to completion.

⛔ **I reported that job as "running and healthy" while it was already dead.** The evidence I used
was the row count rising between two checks, which only proves it *had* been running. The count had
been frozen for 39 minutes.

**Check liveness properly, in this order:**

```bash
date -r checkpoint.jsonl   # last write
date                       # now
pgrep -af myscript         # and beware: your own ssh command string matches the pattern
```

**Why:** a double is usually written from the happy path, so it models what the real object
*accepts* and silently omits what it *rejects*. Every refusal the real object makes is a branch the
caller must handle, and a permissive double deletes all of them at once. The same file already had
this fixed once for `publish` ("RAISES for an uncertified artifact, exactly as
`CalibrationRepository.publish` does") and the lesson was not generalised to its neighbours.

**How to apply:**

**A fake that cannot reproduce the real object's REFUSALS does not test the caller. It tests
itself.** Measured 2026-08-18 on `recall/wizard/pipeline.py`.

`_fail` existed to stop an aborted run stranding a generation. It had a test, a docstring naming the
exact leak, and it had never once worked: `validate` sets state READY, the real
`GenerationManager.fail` refuses READY (`generations.py:681`), and the `InvalidGenerationTransition`
landed in a bare `except Exception: pass` two lines below. `gc` collects only `retired` and `failed`,
so every uncertified build leaked a full copy of the corpus's chunk rows, permanently, on the
**exit-0 success path**.

The concrete instance from that branch: a kwargs-capturing fake let `server_env` ship with a new
parameter **no caller passed**, because the fake accepted anything and the assertion checked what
the fake received. The fix was to stop faking and ask the real destination what it got — drive the
real lifespan against a real database and read `state["store"].table`.

per-checkout database precisely so that "real" is cheap; a double is the expensive option that
looks cheap. Where a double is genuinely necessary, assert against the **effect** it produced, not
against the call it recorded.

  vacuously true, so assert the baseline is non-trivial too.

**Why:** a double is usually written from the happy path, so it models what the real object
*accepts* and silently omits what it *rejects*. Every refusal the real object makes is a branch the
caller must handle, and a permissive double deletes all of them at once. The same file already had
this fixed once for `publish` ("RAISES for an uncertified artifact, exactly as
`CalibrationRepository.publish` does") and the lesson was not generalised to its neighbours.

**How to apply:**

**A fake that cannot reproduce the real object's REFUSALS does not test the caller. It tests
itself.** Measured 2026-08-18 on `recall/wizard/pipeline.py`.

exact leak, and it had never once worked: `validate` sets state READY, the real
`GenerationManager.fail` refuses READY (`generations.py:681`), and the `InvalidGenerationTransition`
landed in a bare `except Exception: pass` two lines below. `gc` collects only `retired` and `failed`,
so every uncertified build leaked a full copy of the corpus's chunk rows, permanently, on the
**exit-0 success path**.

parameter **no caller passed**, because the fake accepted anything and the assertion checked what
the fake received. The fix was to stop faking and ask the real destination what it got — drive the
real lifespan against a real database and read `state["store"].table`.

🔑 **Prefer a real object to a double wherever the real one can be had.** This project has a
per-checkout database precisely so that "real" is cheap; a double is the expensive option that
looks cheap. Where a double is genuinely necessary, assert against the **effect** it produced, not
against the call it recorded.

A green `pytest` and a green `ruff check` in this repository do **not** predict CI. On 2026-08-28
a 54-fix branch passed 593 local tests and then failed four CI checks. Run these before pushing:

```bash
python -m mypy                          # or: make typecheck   (added 2026-08-29)
python scripts/check_citation_anchors.py
python scripts/check_doc_citations.py
python -m pytest tests/test_atm_runner_published.py tests/test_env_example_parity.py -q
```

The version was right and the command was still wrong: I ran `python -m ruff check` on **each file
as I wrote it** and never on the tree. CI runs `ruff check .` and failed with five findings, all in
one new test file, none of which the per-file runs had covered because I never pointed one at that
file.

⛔ **The argument to `ruff check` is part of the command. `python -m ruff check adapters/foo/` is
not a weaker version of the CI check, it is a different check.** Same failure family as the version
gap above and as [[windows-dev-linux-ci-hides-defects-in-both-directions]]: something that looked
like the CI command and was not.

Run the whole thing before pushing, which is also cheap:

```bash
python -m ruff check . && python -m pytest tests/ -q
```

⚠️ Related but distinct from the local-gates problem: [[ruff-blocked-locally]] records that `mypy`
is a second CI gate on files pyflakes calls clean, and this session's FIRST red round was three
mypy errors, because `CLAUDE.md`'s Testing section documents `ruff check` and not `mypy`. Running
one linter and calling the gates clean is a different mistake from running a stale subset, and both
landed in the same push.

## 🔁 Second instance, 2026-08-19, and I did not follow this memo

PR #425. I rebased 18 commits onto a master 48 ahead, ran the four DOC gates I judged relevant
(78 passed), pushed, and opened the PR. **CI went red twice in a row on things the subset could
not see.**

- Round 1: `typecheck`, 10 mypy errors. Exactly the gap

🔑 **A local suite proves the code runs in MY environment, not that it runs.** The two failure modes
are symmetric and both invisible from here: a package I happen to have, and a binary I happen to
have. A test that calls `resolve_claude_executable()` is testing my laptop.

Three rules that follow:

1. **A new import needs a declaration, not just an install.** `import scipy` in shipped code is a
   dependency even when the module is a benchmark helper.
2. **A test that needs an external binary must skip without it**, not fail. `pytest.importorskip`
   and a `shutil.which` guard are the whole fix.
3. **Run what CI runs before pushing**, which here is more than pytest: `python -m mypy`,
   `uv lock --check`, and `pip-audit`. Ruff plus pytest is two of five gates.

| CI check | why it failed | why local missed it |
|---|---|---|
| `test`, `floor` | `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'scipy'` | scipy is installed on this machine; it is **not a declared dependency** |
| `test`, `floor` | `FileNotFoundError: 'claude' is not on PATH` | I have Claude Code installed; the runner does not |
| `typecheck` | 9 mypy errors across `traps.py`, `stats.py`, `claude_exec.py`, `gate.py` | **mypy does not run inside pytest**, and I only ran pytest and ruff |
| `audit` | `uv.lock has drifted from pyproject.toml` | I added an optional extra and did not run `uv lock` |
| `audit` | `pip-audit`: **ragas 0.4.3 → PYSEC-2026-3046** | a new dependency can carry a known CVE, and nothing local checks |

3. **Same command, different ANSWER — 2026-07-30, mem-bench.** I ran `ruff check .` (the gate's
   exact command, per lesson 2) and reported clean. CI failed with **16 errors**. Cause: CI does
   `pip install ruff` *unpinned* → 0.16.0; my machine had 0.6.9. Same command, same scope, two
   years of new default rules. Most findings predated the branch. **An unpinned tool in a
   merge-gating job means the gate's verdict changes with no commit** — a green PR goes red
   tomorrow, and the failure is attributed to whoever happens to push next. Fixed by pinning
   `ruff==0.16.0` in CI and installing that exact version locally to reproduce.
   ⚠️ Two of the 16 needed a *decision*, not compliance: six were in **hash-locked vendored code**
   where "fixing" them breaks the provenance test

Re-measure the gap in two seconds; if the two versions ever agree, this memo is retired:

```bash
ruff --version; python -m ruff --version; cat requirements-dev.txt
```

This is the same shape as [[windows-dev-linux-ci-hides-defects-in-both-directions]]: a green local
check that is not evidence about CI. There the difference was the platform, here it is the version
resolution, and in both cases the local command LOOKED like the CI command.

## A third way to be green locally and red in CI, hit 2026-08-29 on PR #18

⚠️ **Corrected 2026-08-07. The previous version of this memory said ruff cannot launch here
(`os error 4551`, Application Control policy). That is no longer true and following it means
skipping a lint gate that works.**

Verified 2026-08-11, both forms launch:

- `python -m ruff check .` → **ruff 0.16.2**. Use this one. It now matches the repo's declared dev
  range, which #278 raised to `ruff>=0.16,<0.17` on 2026-08-11 (see [[recall-platform-floors]]).
- bare `ruff --version` → **ruff 0.6.9**, a much older install still on PATH.

**Why it matters:** RE-call's CI runs `ruff check .` as a hard gate in the `test` job, and it runs
**before pytest**, so the whole `test` job dies at lint and a green local pytest tells you nothing.
Two separate misses so far, both on files pyflakes called clean:

🔑 **The fix for 2 is a scoped `[[tool.mypy.overrides]]`, NOT an inline `# type: ignore`**, when the
config sets `warn_unused_ignores = true`: the inline ignore is UNUSED for anyone who does have the
module importable, so it fails precisely the developer best placed to run the code.

## How to apply

- Before pushing anything under a directory with sweep-style guards, run the **full** suite once, or
  at minimum grep for tests whose names describe the PACKAGE (`no_*_without_*`, `every_*`, `all_*`).
- Run `python -m mypy` locally before claiming a branch is clean. "ruff passed" is true and
  incomplete.
- Read CI's job list rather than assuming `test` is the only gate. This repo has twelve.

Why it mattered rather than being a lint: `benchmarks.run` marks a refused artifact **in band**, and
a refused file is byte-identical to a real measurement to anything ignoring the mark. The script
validated itself against a run's published score, so an unchecked read would let a **quarantined run
become the baseline the check passes against** — the apparatus check turning into a rubber stamp
exactly in the case it exists for.

**2. `ruff check` is not a type check.** CI runs `mypy` as a separate job. A deliberately-external
import (an evaluator supplied at run time via a `--root` flag, never a dependency) is invisible to
ruff and red to mypy.

**1. mypy is a separate gate and ruff says nothing about it.** `typecheck` runs `python -m mypy`
over 349 files, about 60 seconds. The three errors that got through were a `tuple(x)` call
widening `tuple[float, float]` to `tuple[float, ...]`, and two `getattr` results that narrow at
runtime but not for the checker. As of 2026-08-29 `CLAUDE.md` documents it and `make typecheck`
exists; before that, nothing in the repo told a session mypy was a gate.

**How to apply:** before trusting a scoped check, **print what the scope matched** (`| wc -l`,
`--name-only`). And run the verification command the *gate* runs, not a convenient subset of it —
if CI runs `ruff check .`, run `ruff check .`. A narrower check than the gate is not a check.
Then the third axis: **check the gate's tool VERSION too.** `pip install <tool>` with no pin is
itself the defect — pin it, and run that pinned version locally (a throwaway venv is enough).
"Same command" is not "same answer".

The recovery is the other half of the lesson: the audit dispatched to cover the missed test files
produced the single best finding of the run — a test guarding "the label must never be a lie" that
passed vacuously, proven by mutation. The gap was worth closing, not noting.

Measured 2026-08-29 on PR #13: `ruff check .` printed "All checks passed!" here and CI went red in
9 seconds, twice, on four findings the older binary does not know about (TRY004, RUF100 twice,
I001).

The cause is two ruffs. `requirements-dev.txt` pins **ruff 0.16.2**, which is what CI installs and
what `python -m ruff` resolves to in this checkout. The `ruff` on PATH is **0.6.9**, stale, and its
default rule set is narrower. Both answer to the same command name, neither says which it is, and
the newer one is the one that decides whether the branch is mergeable.

⚠️ The `ruff check .` line in this repository's own docs and in the CI workflow is therefore a
trap when read as a local instruction. Run it as a module:

```bash
python -m ruff check . && python -m ruff --version
```

# What this records

PR 91, `Add RE-call lifecycle capability support`, is on branch `codex/xerj`. Its merge conflict
