query.query: Why can a busy machine make database coverage disappear while the suite stays green?

pool.text:
🔑 **The mechanism, in one line:** `tests/conftest.py` decided "is there a database" by opening a
connection with `connect_timeout=2`, and `require_db()` called it **per test**, uncached. On a
loaded host a probe loses that race, and `require_db()` responds to a lost race by **skipping**.

⛔ **This is a false GREEN, which is why it survived.** A flake that produces a red gets chased. A
flake that produces a skip produces a passing run, and the only trace is a skip count nobody
compares between runs. `CLAUDE.md` already warned "read the skip count before calling a run green"
and named several hundred as the danger signal; 88 against 34 is well under that and still lost a
quarter of the database coverage.

**How to apply:**
1. A suite verdict is the SUMMARY LINE, never an exit code. An output file with no pytest output
   means "did not run or was lost", whatever the code says.
2. Launch long suites detached with their own log (`nohup python -u -m pytest tests/ -q > log
   2>&1 &`, the `-u` matters or the log stays empty for minutes) and watch the log with a
   Monitor until-loop for the summary line.
3. Before relaunching anything DB-backed, list live python processes and match COMMAND LINES:
   two suites on one session database invalidate each other silently.
4. Distinguish your processes from other sessions' by command line before killing: this machine
   routinely runs parallel sessions with their own suites.

⚠️ **CI skip counts are NOT comparable to local ones.** The same commit reports `6129 passed, 107
skipped` on CI, higher than either local run, because CI has no Voyage or OpenAI keys. So "CI skips
more than me" is normal and proves nothing either way. Compare a machine against **itself**.

**The fix, and the part that is not obvious.** Memoise the probe, so the answer is decided once at
conftest import before the suite can load the machine; give a *configured* database 10 seconds and
up to three attempts, because one decision for a whole run must not itself be a coin flip; and put
the failure text into the skip reason, because "nothing is listening" and "something is there and
too slow" want opposite responses from whoever reads the report.

replacing CLAUDE.md](adding-recall-beats-replacing-claude-md.md) — measured: additive gives 0 of 40 hazards and roughly doubled correctness; substitutional gives neither. Plus the cost, which goes the other way.
- [A loaded machine turns DB tests into green skips](a-loaded-machine-turns-db-tests-into-green-skips.md) — the suite re-probed the database per test with a 2 second timeout, so a busy host silently converted 54 passing DB tests into skips. Same commit, same container: 34 skips idle, 88 loaded, zero failures either way. Compare a machine against itself; CI skip counts are not comparable.
- [The anchor checker cannot see inside a function](anchor-checker-cannot-see-inside-a-function.md) — its window is a whole function body, so `def promote` and a line in promote's body both pass.

🔑 **Retry ambiguity, never certainty.** A refused connection is a complete answer and must not be
retried. That is not tidiness: `tests/test_requires_db_coverage.py` deliberately runs a subprocess
against a dead port and requires a clean skip, so retrying refusals triples the fixed cost of the
guard protecting the whole fixture set. Measured on the new test file, 26.9s before the
short-circuit and 1.4s after.

I put a marker on a corpus-relative path; `supersedes_key` keeps only the last segment, so the
marker survived for `bad.md` and was stripped for `sub/bad.md`. Every test used a root-level file,
so the suite stayed green while nested corpora were broken. I fixed it, and the very next guard
(`startswith` on that marker) had the identical hole, also invisible at the root. An audit found
both; my tests could not have.

**Why:** a normaliser that reduces structure (last segment, basename, stem) makes position part of
the input. A fixture that only ever builds files at the root never varies the one dimension the
code is sensitive to, so the tests agree with the bug.

**Prefer impossible over detectable.** A static guard proving every DB test carried `@requires_db`
was wrong three times, each caught by an auditor: it hid 161 of 363 tests behind wrapper fixtures,
then 17 more, then misclassified 227 locals, always green while the property went unchecked over
a growing share of the suite, because I derived truth from a hand-written list and kept widening
it. Making `make_store` call `pytest.skip()` deleted 574 lines of inference, is exact rather than
approximate, and protects the tests whose author forgot the mark, the entire population at risk.
Ask early: can I make this impossible instead of detectable?

Cost: about 40 minutes of wall clock and one contaminated run, caught before any conclusion
rested on it.

## 🔁 Second instance, 2026-09-01: `gh run watch`, and this time the file was NOT empty

Same false green, different tool, and the new detail is that **the output file looked healthy**.

`gh run list ... | xargs gh run watch <id> --exit-status`, backgrounded, notified "completed
(exit code 0)" with a **950-byte** output file full of green ticks. It contained exactly two
jobs, `typecheck` and `Schema migrations (PostgreSQL 16)`, then `[exited with code 0]`. The three
jobs that actually matter here, `test`, `floor` and `Clean install (wizard)`, were still pending
when the watch exited and appear nowhere in it. The watcher had attached to a partial view and
returned.

1. **CI runs the whole suite in 4:19** (6,623 passed, 151 skipped, `-n auto` with coverage,
   run 32966542600). The suite is large, not slow.
2. **Every real-model test together is 73 tests and 80.35s serial**, slowest single test 5.26s:
   all `requires_fastembed`, the QNLI entailment judge, the sentence-transformers reranker.
   They run only locally; CI installs without those extras, which is its 151 skips against a
   healthy local 34.
3. **What actually produces >40 minute local runs**: either a serial run (~50 min by
   construction, no hotspot, see [[test-suite-runs-in-parallel-now]]) or `-n 4` on a loaded box,
   where workers are OOM-killed and retried. The processes hogging the machine during those runs
   were other sessions' local `recall.cli index` / benchmark embedding runs

⚠️ **CI is the arbiter, not this box.** The GitHub runner gets a private database and no competing
session; both PRs (#234, #239) went green there on `test` while the local suite still showed
collisions. 12 worktrees share this clone → [[feedback-concurrent-sessions-race-the-same-clone-2026-07-24]].

🔑 **Write the expected pass count BEFORE the run.** "3115 passed, 0 failed" reads as success; only
a committed prediction of 3117 made the gap visible, and that gap is what led to this diagnosis.

The mechanism that came out of it: `scripts/suite-preflight.sh`, called by `make test`, sizes the
worker count from memory actually available (≥6 GB → 4, ≥3 GB → 2, else serial), warns about
competing pytest/indexing processes by command line, and is overridden verbatim by `N=<n>`.
Mutation-tested via `scripts/suite_preflight_tests.sh`. One trap it encodes: **Git Bash emulates
`/proc/meminfo` WITHOUT a MemAvailable line**, so a probe that trusts the file's existence reads
Windows as "unknown memory" forever; the script falls through to PowerShell's
`Win32_PerfFormattedData_PerfOS_Memory.AvailableMBytes`, which matches Task Manager's
"Available".

Related: [[a-buffered-pipe-makes-a-live-run-look-hung]],
[[background-suite-exit-0-with-empty-output-is-not-green]].

🔑 **The competing process is usually one I started myself.** A `bug-auditor` subagent runs pytest.
Chaining `pytest A && pytest B` overlaps if the first has not fully released its connections. Both
happened repeatedly, and I diagnosed the results as broken apparatus, code regression, catalog
bloat and machine contention before noticing I was the other party. **Tell subagents explicitly not
to touch the database, and never run a suite while one is live.**

🔑 **The failing test set CHANGES every run** and each one passes in isolation, which reads exactly
like order-dependent shared state. There is no randomiser installed — it is whichever test happened
to be migrating when the lock was taken.

manual run found in seconds: a config `load_config` refused, a runtime whose `list_tenants` raised on a started runtime, a `waitForDone()` with no timeout. Cross the seam once by hand, then encode it.
- [Deleting a function deletes its side effects](deleting-a-function-deletes-its-side-effects.md) — `03456359` removed `write_mcp_config` and with it the only `mkdir` that created `project_root`; a whole green suite missed it because every fixture pre-created the directory. Grep for what a body WROTE, not only for its callers.
- [An empty assertion can pass vacuously after you change an accumulator](an-empty-assertion-can-pass-vacuously-after-you-change-an-accumulator.md) — `== ()` stayed green across a real fix because the fixture never reached the other producer; ask why the value is

🔑 **The test that would have caught this is a COUNT, not a shape.** The suite is ~7,100 tests;
any summary line whose passed+failed+skipped total is not in that ballpark is a non-run however
well formed it looks. CLAUDE.md already says "read the skip count before calling a run green" for
the 34-versus-several-hundred case; the same arithmetic catches this one, and it is the only rule
in this memo that does.

sample then breaking/capping silently keeps only its head. Made this EXACT mistake twice in one package, same numbers both times (3 of 51 files). Assert COVERAGE, not count.

Measured 2026-08-20 in recall, at a cost of one 45-minute suite run killed at 43%.

`scripts/session-db.sh up` derives the container name from a hash of the checkout path, so the
container for `.claude/worktrees/agent-memory-recall-research-9ab019` was `recall-sess-0cd0d974`
whichever session started it. Another session claimed that worktree mid-run (see
[[sessionstart-hook-claims-workspaces]]), and its teardown removed *my* container while my `pytest`
was still using it.

## What the failure looks like, and why it misleads

Staging by pathspec is the house rule (whole-tree adds are blocked because sessions share
clones), and on 2026-08-22 it produced its own failure mode: the agent-memory-bench Phase 1
commit staged `tasks/ oracles/ corpus/ scripts/ harness/` but not `tests/`, so
`tests/test_references.py` (72 discrimination assertions) stayed untracked. CI ran green in
14 seconds on 61 tests; locally the receipt said 133. The suite that gates the work shipped
without its gate, and the green was real, just about the wrong set.

**Why:** a pathspec list encodes what you remembered changing, and new test files are the
thing most often forgotten because the habit is "code changed, tests changed beside it";
here the tests were NEW files in a directory not named in the list.

- **A unit test that a verifier rejects a bad token does not prove the SDK ever calls it.** All 52
  auth unit tests would have stayed green with `token_verifier` dropped and the server wide open.
  Only a live server making real HTTP requests settles it — and the authenticated *control* is
  required, or a server rejecting everything also passes. Same family as
  [[feedback-exercise-the-detection-path-not-the-green-path-2026-07-22]].
- `FASTMCP_PORT` is read when the `FastMCP` object is constructed at **import** time and is
  silently ignored if set later — RE-call now exposes `RECALL_HOST`/`RECALL_PORT` instead.

⚠️ **Second, unrelated trap the same day: a background suite does not survive its session.** A
serial run launched in one session was killed at 54% by session teardown, and the
`SessionEnd` hook had already removed this checkout's DB container, so the log ended in large
consecutive blocks of `F` and `E`. **A cascade is diagnostic**: scattered failures are a code
problem, contiguous blocks are a shared resource that went away. A fresh container plus a rerun
inside one session was clean to 57% with zero failures.

Cost: about 90 minutes of wall clock across three non-runs, and zero wrong conclusions, because
CI was used as the authoritative gate instead (`7139 passed, 173 skipped`, twice).

🔑 **Runtime is the tell.** A full suite is ~11 min; 3 s across a whole file is a setup failure,
and ~3 min for the whole suite means it never really ran.

## Diagnosing it, cheaply

- `grep -c ConcurrentMigrator <captured output>` — report the count as a NUMBER, do not infer it.
- `-rf` lists failures but **NOT errors**; use `-ra` or the error is silently withheld from you.
- **Capture to a file.** `| tail -5` twice cost a round each: the traceback that names the cause
  was thrown away, and I reasoned about failures I could not see.
- Check `select count(*) from pg_locks where locktype='advisory'` BEFORE starting, and count
  python processes. Zero at start is not a guarantee — another session can begin mid-run.

⚠️ The tempting fix was the wrong one: register `13c` in the crossref test's `EXPECTED` table and
the gate goes green. That makes a pointer to nothing *valid*. Repoint by name instead.

Related: [[a-green-local-suite-hid-four-ci-gates]], [[two-citation-gates-freeze-differently]],
[[guards-that-cannot-fail]].

| observed | I nearly concluded | actually |
|---|---|---|
| full suite: 23 failed / 16 errors | my new DB-creating fixture polluted the suite | two full suites running CONCURRENTLY, both driving the same `recall-e2e` container the suite spins up |
| same files on a fresh `git worktree` of master: 34 errors in **3.4s** | the failures are pre-existing on master | a bare worktree has no local environment; it errored at *setup*. Not a baseline. |
| suite with my files deselected: **3093 errors** | catastrophic breakage | still overlapping with another run |

One clean run, nothing else touching Docker: **3107 passed, 18 skipped, 0 failed.**

🔑 **A 3.4-second failure across a whole file is a setup failure, not a code failure.** The
runtime is the tell.

The one hop database byte p95 was 455355 versus 149016 for graph off, so remaining graph database
work is the next optimization target. The locked cold versus warm graph stage p95 gate remains
pending because only one cold projection sample exists.

The DeepSeek V4 Flash replay had zero provider failures. Valid answer rate and correct abstention
were unchanged. Complete gold citation coverage rose from 0.020 to 0.080 and mean gold citation
recall rose from 0.205 to 0.271, while any gold citation stayed at 0.220 and mean citation
precision fell from 0.520 to 0.482. This is evidence quality only, not factual correctness, and
the quality differences are caused by one hop evidence selection rather than projection caching.

🔑 **The 2026-08-23 rule said an output file with no output means "did not run".** That was too
narrow. A file with plenty of output can still be a partial view, so the test is not "is the file
empty" but **"does the file contain a verdict for every unit I care about"**. Fifteen checks
existed; the file named two.

What I did instead, and what the answer must always come from, is the SERVICE rather than the
watcher:

```bash
gh pr checks <n> --json name,state -q '.[] | select(.state != "SUCCESS") | .name'
```

**A green local suite here is not evidence about CI, and a green CI is not evidence about a real
run.** The harness is developed on Windows and `ci.yml` runs `ubuntu-latest`; the Docker image is
`python:3.12-slim`, so the platform the benchmark *ships to* is the one the dev machine is not.

Three defects on 2026-08-28, each invisible on one side:

baseline_items.text:
🔑 **The mechanism, in one line:** `tests/conftest.py` decided "is there a database" by opening a
connection with `connect_timeout=2`, and `require_db()` called it **per test**, uncached. On a
loaded host a probe loses that race, and `require_db()` responds to a lost race by **skipping**.

⛔ **This is a false GREEN, which is why it survived.** A flake that produces a red gets chased. A
flake that produces a skip produces a passing run, and the only trace is a skip count nobody
compares between runs. `CLAUDE.md` already warned "read the skip count before calling a run green"
and named several hundred as the danger signal; 88 against 34 is well under that and still lost a
quarter of the database coverage.

**How to apply:**
1. A suite verdict is the SUMMARY LINE, never an exit code. An output file with no pytest output
   means "did not run or was lost", whatever the code says.
2. Launch long suites detached with their own log (`nohup python -u -m pytest tests/ -q > log
   2>&1 &`, the `-u` matters or the log stays empty for minutes) and watch the log with a
   Monitor until-loop for the summary line.
3. Before relaunching anything DB-backed, list live python processes and match COMMAND LINES:
   two suites on one session database invalidate each other silently.
4. Distinguish your processes from other sessions' by command line before killing: this machine
   routinely runs parallel sessions with their own suites.

⚠️ **CI skip counts are NOT comparable to local ones.** The same commit reports `6129 passed, 107
skipped` on CI, higher than either local run, because CI has no Voyage or OpenAI keys. So "CI skips
more than me" is normal and proves nothing either way. Compare a machine against **itself**.

**The fix, and the part that is not obvious.** Memoise the probe, so the answer is decided once at
conftest import before the suite can load the machine; give a *configured* database 10 seconds and
up to three attempts, because one decision for a whole run must not itself be a coin flip; and put
the failure text into the skip reason, because "nothing is listening" and "something is there and
too slow" want opposite responses from whoever reads the report.

🔑 **Retry ambiguity, never certainty.** A refused connection is a complete answer and must not be
retried. That is not tidiness: `tests/test_requires_db_coverage.py` deliberately runs a subprocess
against a dead port and requires a clean skip, so retrying refusals triples the fixed cost of the
guard protecting the whole fixture set. Measured on the new test file, 26.9s before the
short-circuit and 1.4s after.

query.query: Before fixing an infrastructure bug from this checkout, what freshness check prevents rebuilding an old fix?

pool.text:
**A stale worktree does not announce itself, and it makes fixed bugs look live.** The stale
checkout held the stale `.mcp.json`, so the artifact and the code that generates it were wrong
*together*, consistently, with no contradiction visible from inside. Every observation I made was
correct. The conclusion was wrong because the frame was.

This is the same failure the global notes already describe under "a checkout old enough to lack
`CLAUDE-lessons.md` is exactly the stale shared one", and under `session-open.sh` failing closed
when `session-space.sh` is missing. I did not run `session-open.sh` at the start of this session,
which is precisely what would have printed `32 commit(s) behind`.

A bug report that names a **directory, a file and an observed symptom** reads as current, and in a
clone with twenty worktrees it often is not. Detail is not freshness. The first question is not
"what writes this?" but "**is the fix already in the checkout that saw it?**"

```bash
git log --oneline -5 -- <suspect-path>          # has this been touched recently?
git merge-base --is-ancestor <fix-sha> <reporting-worktree-HEAD> && echo IN || echo BEHIND
```

The tell that generalises: **five checkouts held leftover `uploads/` directories, and the residue
outlives the fix.** A stale artifact on disk keeps testifying to a bug that no longer exists, so
"the directory is right there" is evidence of a past run, not of present behaviour.

**Why:** re-fixing a fixed bug is worse than wasted time. It lands a duplicate control, and the two
disagree the moment one is edited; the guard test that already exists then fails and reads as the
new work being wrong.

1. **Before diagnosing any infrastructure fault, print the distance to `origin/master`.** One
   command, and it is the difference between a fix and a reimplementation:
   `git fetch -q origin && git rev-list --count HEAD..origin/master`
2. **Before writing a script into `scripts/`, list what is already there on master**, not in your
   checkout: `git ls-tree --name-only origin/master scripts/`. I would have seen
   `session-corpus.sh` immediately.
3. **Treat a merge conflict on a file you rewrote as evidence about the world**, not an obstacle.
   The conflict was the first true thing this session learned about the state of the repository.
4. **Run `scripts/session-open.sh` at the start of a session in this repository.** It prints the
   distance, and it fails closed on a stale checkout

ignoring the legacy ENDPOINT sends the key to a default nobody chose; a shared validator inherits the weakest caller's assumptions.
- [Forcing the call does not force the mechanism](forcing-the-call-does-not-force-the-mechanism.md) — a component with no input still runs and still returns a number; check the mechanism has input, name which mechanism, and add the A-minus-B control arm.
- [A memory outage conceals the memo that would fix it](a-memory-outage-conceals-the-memo-that-would-fix-it.md) — I rebuilt recall's MCP fix from a worktree 32 commits behind; master had shipped it five days earlier in #514. A stale checkout makes a fixed bug look live, because the config and the code that writes it are wrong together. Check the distance to origin/master before diagnosing infrastructure.

## CCA drift fixed
The project-local `.claude/commands/audit-fix.md` (worktree + main checkout) was
the OLD 6-layer version, shadowing the global tiered one (project scope wins).
Deleted both stale copies → one source of truth (global). `.claude/` is
gitignored; backups at `C:\bugsmash\cca-stale-backup`. **CCA has NO version
number** (the "3.2/3.3" the user half-remembers is the public `cca_checks`
package "v3.0-min", PR #6 — not the pipeline). User will version-stamp the
pipeline in a dedicated session.

KEY: **`cca_checks` is installed EDITABLE from the clone** — `import cca_checks` resolves inside
`Documents/cca-audit/cca_checks`. So the Python side needs no sync, but it follows whatever branch
the clone is checked out on. Leave the clone on `master`, or a stray checkout silently changes what
every audit runs.

## The Hypothesis banner bug (found by CI, fixed in #21)

`property_check.py` keyed CONFIRMED on `Falsifying example:`. Hypothesis renamed it to
`Failing test case:` in **6.159.0**. On 6.159+ every numeric finding degraded to UNCERTAIN — the
confirmation path was dead and silent. Local was green (6.158 pinned), CI red (resolved 6.159).
Detail + the generalisable lesson: [[feedback-parsing-tool-output-is-version-fragile-2026-07-21]].

It prints the
   distance, and it fails closed on a stale checkout on purpose.

## What survived

Nothing of the config work; PR #550 is closed with the reasoning in it. What did survive is
unrelated to recall's own servers: the benchmark's interpreter was pinned to `8f6b5d1f` so #549's
embedding cache reaches it, which is a real 79.8% saving on the official-002 tenant build, recorded
as an amendment to preregistration 021.

See also [[squash-merging-forks-every-outstanding-branch]] and
[[another-session-may-be-building-the-same-feature]], which is this failure between two live
sessions rather than between a session and master.

## Oracle snapshot_ts — checked, NOT a bug
Initial `now()-max(snapshot_ts)=−15s` was an anomalous row in the 1h window. Real picture: chainlink BTC snapshots are **3–22s old (median 13s)** because `snapshot_ts` is the on-chain CHAINLINK ROUND time (BTC updates on deviation/heartbeat, not continuously). `_chainlink_now`'s `>now()-5s` filter is a FEATURE — the sniper fires only on a FRESH oracle round (= the oracle just moved vs the lagging PM book), which is exactly the edge. So the "fast feed" (PR&R p50 17ms) is ingest SPEED (how fast we record a new round), not round FREQUENCY. No staleness bug; no resolve-attribution corruption.

**Why:** infrastructure bugs are the class where staleness is most expensive, because config,
scripts and docs all move together and a behind-checkout is internally consistent. A logic bug in
one file shows up against tests; a stale infrastructure frame shows up against nothing.

**How to apply:**

— a 40-pt "memorization gap."** Specificity 12/12 → 9/10. **fp-check drop rate 17%→42%**
  (gate works hardest on novel code = the product thesis, measured).
- Fresh corpus = recent bug-fix PRs (post-Feb-2026) mined via `gh` with a regression-test filter;
  recognition probe certifies cleanliness (famous≠recognized — aiohttp/pipx read clean at code level).
- Write-up: `cca-audit/docs/blog-benchmark-memorization-gap.md` (community-first: "your AI auditor's
  benchmark score is inflated"). Clean catches link real PRs (aiohttp #12264, clu-comics #389, pipx #1860).
- ⚠️ pilot n small (3/7 wide CI); gate dropped 1 REAL catch (satpy #3367); 1 false alarm (clu-comics).
  **Next to firm up: scale to ~30 clean bugs.** Also pending: publish post (dev.to — needs user go-ahead), swap README GIF.

Back to [MEMORY.md](MEMORY.md) and [feedback_index.md](feedback_index.md).

**I rebuilt a fix that already existed, because the checkout I diagnosed from was 32 commits
behind, and the same staleness is what made the bug look live.**

⚠️ **This memo was rewritten within hours of being written, and the first version was wrong in the
direction that flattered me.** It said recall's MCP servers "had been dead for days from three
faults already written down in memory", and framed the lesson as *a memory outage conceals its own
fix*. That framing is seductive and it was not the story. The real story is duller and more useful.

## What actually happened

**The obvious repair is worse than the bug.** Unlinking the stale file and then
competing for the same exclusive create looks correct and is not: the second
racer's `unlink` deletes the **winner's** freshly written claim, and then it
creates its own. I wrote that fix, and only the regression test caught it.

**What actually works:** hold a lock across read, decide and write. `os.mkdir` /
`mkdir` is the atomic primitive available everywhere. A check taken *before* the
lock is a check about the past.

**How to apply:** when a report cites a worktree, resolve that worktree's HEAD before reading any
source. If the fix is present, say so and merge master into the reporting checkout rather than
writing code. If it is absent, the report is live and the hunt is real. Repair is `git merge
origin/master` **in the reporting worktree** and nowhere else: merging master elsewhere does not
reach it. Verify by re-running the suite there and counting the artifacts before and after, not by
reading the diff. And `git fetch` again immediately before committing and again before opening a
PR: the window that matters is the one that opened while you were working, not the one you
checked at the start. Related: [[autouse-fixtures-must-not-write-into-tmp-path]],
[[guards-that-cannot-fail]],

⚠️ Turning production mode on is not free and not only a gate change: it also selects

## Goal & method

query.query: When adding an optional scope keyword to a duck typed store, how should ordinary calls remain compatible?

pool.text:
Back to [MEMORY.md](MEMORY.md) and [feedback_index.md](feedback_index.md).

**Adding a keyword argument to a store or retriever method breaks every duck-typed stand-in in
the suite, on queries that do not use the new feature at all.** Measured 2026-08-29 while adding
folder/facet scoping: `grep -rn "def query_dense" tests/` found **11** doubles with the signature
`(self, vector, k, source=None)`, and passing `scope=` unconditionally from
`HybridRetriever._retrieve_legs` failed 9 of them. The same shape repeated one layer up: five fake
RETRIEVERS with `search(query, k, source)` failed when `recall.trust._trusted_search` passed
`scope=`.

**The fix is not to update the doubles.** It is to send the new keyword only when it carries
information the old one could not:

Both call sites resolve to the same `Scope` inside `PgVectorStore` via `recall.scope.coerce_scope`,
so this is one behaviour reached by two keywords, not two behaviours. `coerce_scope` refuses
`scope=` and `source=` together rather than merging them.

⚠️ **The generalisation is about DUCK TYPING, not about tests.** The signal that a method needs
this treatment is that its parameter is annotated with a concrete class the code never actually
requires: `HybridRetriever._store` is typed `PgVectorStore` and is routinely something else. Where
the type is enforced (a `@dataclass`, a sealed protocol) just add the argument.

Related: [[missing-input-becomes-a-clean-null]], on the other way an interface change goes quiet.

1. **recall is published on PyPI**, so a store or retriever implemented downstream is not
   hypothetical. The eleven doubles are evidence of how easy that interface is to implement, not a
   special property of the test suite.
2. **The failure lands where it is informative.** A store that has not been taught the keyword now
   fails only when a folder or facet is actually requested, which is precisely the call it cannot
   serve. Under the unconditional form it failed on every ordinary query, which is a cost paid by
   callers who asked for nothing.

— recall's `_BODY_RULE_VERSION` docstring diagnosed the general "stale forever" mechanism and then guarded one instance; the facet change hit the same mechanism weeks later and reached 0.3% of a 10,155-chunk corpus. If your docstring describes a class and your guard fires on a member, that gap is the next incident.
- [The apparatus fails toward a finding](the-apparatus-fails-toward-a-finding.md) — four tools in one session each returned a confident FALSE NEGATIVE that read as a result about the code, and every one was caught by a control run rather than by reading harder. A negative ends an investigation, so a false one is absorbed silently.
- [A new keyword breaks every duck-typed double](a-new-keyword-breaks-every-duck-typed-double.md) — adding `scope=` to `query_dense` failed 9 of 11

— adding `scope=` to `query_dense` failed 9 of 11 store doubles and 5 retriever doubles on queries that used no scoping; recall is on PyPI so downstream implementations exist too. Send the new keyword only when it says what the old one could not.
- [Look for recorded ground truth before manufacturing one](look-for-recorded-ground-truth-before-manufacturing-one.md) — I escalated through one judge, then three, then a human labelling sheet, while an executable oracle sat in the same archive; it settled in seconds what four judges could not and supplied the objective NEGATIVES no judge can produce.
- [A single-judge label is not a measurement](a-single-judge-label-is-not-a-measurement.md) — three models on the SAME 46 items with the SAME prompt implied recalls of 10, 9 and 6 of 14; the

- **Judge a candidate scope by the NEAR competition it removes**, not by the fraction of the corpus
  it deletes. Those two numbers came apart by a factor of two here and pointed opposite ways.
- **Measure it before building.** The metric is cheap: take the misses, look at what actually
  occupies their top-k, and ask how much of it the scope would remove. That single number would
  have predicted this null without writing the arm.
- A scope that cuts ACROSS the natural clustering (a facet, an authority tier, a date band) can
  reach competition that a scope aligned WITH it cannot.

⛔ **Both arms were oracles**, handed the folder or facet containing the answer. 15% is a ceiling,
not a feature; anything shippable has to infer the scope and nothing here says it can.

A `recall/` memo is outranked mostly by *other `recall/` memos*. Deleting 82% of the corpus removed
39% of the actual competition and left every memo losing to the same folder-mates it was already
losing to. The facet scope thins `recall/` itself, which is why the scope that looked weaker is the
only one that rescued anything.

## How to apply it

> Every memo appears in exactly one sub-index. The groups above are a **second** view of the

Back to [MEMORY.md](MEMORY.md) and [feedback_index.md](feedback_index.md).

**Adding a keyword argument to a store or retriever method breaks every duck-typed stand-in in
the suite, on queries that do not use the new feature at all.** Measured 2026-08-29 while adding
folder/facet scoping: `grep -rn "def query_dense" tests/` found **11** doubles with the signature
`(self, vector, k, source=None)`, and passing `scope=` unconditionally from
`HybridRetriever._retrieve_legs` failed 9 of them. The same shape repeated one layer up: five fake
RETRIEVERS with `search(query, k, source)` failed when `recall.trust._trusted_search` passed
`scope=`.

**The fix is not to update the doubles.** It is to send the new keyword only when it carries
information the old one could not:

Both call sites resolve to the same `Scope` inside `PgVectorStore` via `recall.scope.coerce_scope`,
so this is one behaviour reached by two keywords, not two behaviours. `coerce_scope` refuses
`scope=` and `source=` together rather than merging them.

⚠️ **The generalisation is about DUCK TYPING, not about tests.** The signal that a method needs
this treatment is that its parameter is annotated with a concrete class the code never actually
requires: `HybridRetriever._store` is typed `PgVectorStore` and is routinely something else. Where
the type is enforced (a `@dataclass`, a sealed protocol) just add the argument.

Related: [[missing-input-becomes-a-clean-null]], on the other way an interface change goes quiet.

1. **recall is published on PyPI**, so a store or retriever implemented downstream is not
   hypothetical. The eleven doubles are evidence of how easy that interface is to implement, not a
   special property of the test suite.
2. **The failure lands where it is informative.** A store that has not been taught the keyword now
   fails only when a folder or facet is actually requested, which is precisely the call it cannot
   serve. Under the unconditional form it failed on every ordinary query, which is a cost paid by
   callers who asked for nothing.

query.query: What extra apparatus check prevents a broken treatment arm from looking like a genuine null?

pool.text:
⛔ **The apparatus gate did not catch any of them, and it PASSED (14/14 and 26/26).** That is the
part worth internalising: the gate examined only the CONTROL arm. A baseline that faithfully
reproduces a prior run says nothing about whether the treatment was ever applied. In this run the
treatment genuinely was live, and the only evidence of that was a divergence check I happened to
run by hand afterwards and paste into the result section. Had I not, a fabricated null and a real
one would have been indistinguishable in the artifact, in the record, and in the memo.

**How to apply, and this is the general rule for any experiment with a preferred-cheap outcome:**

- **Assert the TREATMENT is live, not just that the baseline reproduces.** A control-only gate is
  half a gate. Require the treated arm to differ from control on some minimum fraction of cases,
  and void the run when it does not.
- **Enumerate the ways your instrument could produce your expected result while broken.** If the
  list is long and the expected result is a null, the experiment is measuring your apparatus.
  Write that list into the pre-registration before running.
- **A gate with both halves of every ratio.** "At least 13 of 14" enforced as `>= 13` is a
  different gate the moment the denominator moves; assert the denominator too.
- **Fail loudly on the cheap path.** A void run that exits 0 and prints its tables is a verdict to
  anything downstream. Non-zero exit, and a

almost
never right: the absent field means the measurement did not happen, and a null result is exactly
what a broken measurement looks like. Read with `[...]` and let it raise.

**The tell**: a metric landing on the theoretical no-signal value EXACTLY. 0.500 for AUC, 0.0 for a
rate, 1.00 for a ratio. Real data rarely hits the null value to four decimals. When it does, check
that the input exists before believing the result.

⚠️ **A partial failure is worse than a total one.** If the join fails for some rows only, those get
zeroed features while the rest are real, which manufactures a split in every affected feature
rather than flattening it. Total failure at least looks like nothing; partial failure looks like a
finding.

**Fourth instance, 2026-08-22, and it inflated a

| broken thing | why the output is identical to a real null |
|---|---|
| an arm pointed at the control DSN | control reproduced every miss, so an arm that IS control cannot rescue and must retain |
| an `--exclude-base` matching nothing | denominators shift, thresholds do not, verdict still prints |
| a gate applied to the wrong population | 13-of-14 becomes 13-of-15 and still clears |
| an empty or mis-keyed query set | nothing retrieves, so nothing is rescued |

🔑 **The transferable lesson, and the reason this correction is worth more than the fixes: every
one of those 14 defects fails TOWARD the published answer.** Four independent paths in that
apparatus print `rescue 0/14, retention 26/26` exactly: an arm pointed at control, an exclusion
matching nothing, a gate applied to the wrong denominator, an empty query set. A null is the
cheapest result an instrument can fabricate, and a passing apparatus gate does not protect against
it when the gate only ever examines the control arm. The run survived because a divergence check
was done by hand afterwards. **When a measurement can only come out one way if it breaks, assert
the treatment is live, not just that the baseline reproduces.** Fixes and tests:
`scripts/agent_ab_discoverability_tests.py`, [PR

- **Assert the TREATMENT is live, not just that the baseline reproduces.** A control-only gate is

- **A gate with both halves of every ratio.** "At least 13 of 14" enforced as `>= 13` is a
  different gate the moment the denominator moves; assert the denominator too.
- **Fail loudly on the cheap path.** A void run that exits 0 and prints its tables is a verdict to
  anything downstream. Non-zero exit, and a

recall tools, and a transcript that otherwise reads normally. In an A/B that is an on arm silently
losing its treatment and averaging in as evidence the treatment does nothing. The admission gate
caught it here; without one it would have been 48 null pairs. See

**And check the tool list, not the exit status.** All three of these produced a session that ran to
completion and reported success with the tool simply absent; see

Measured 2026-08-25 from `results/pilot-004-placebo/records.final.jsonl` in file (run) order: the
eight recall sessions whose MCP server reported `status: failed` sit at positions 4, 5, 7, 9, 13,
34, 36 and 37 of the seventy-two recall sessions. None in the last thirty-four. Two bursts,
uncorrelated with tasks. `mcp_server_errors` was `[]` in all eight, so the run recorded that the
server had failed and could not say why.

Measured the same day by driving the real server over stdio with the new preflight probe: the
recall MCP server takes **12.3 seconds** to answer `initialize` then `tools/list`, and lists 18
tools. That matches the 13 seconds `harness/gate.py` names in its docstring as the original cause,
so the race is real and the window is wide.

Measured 2026-08-26 during `diagnostic-002`. Free physical memory was **421 MB of 12,279**. The
recall arm wired for its first six sessions and then failed nearly every one after: `WWWWWW` then
`X` almost continuously. Two cells (`ts-base36-id` seeds 1 and 2) burned all three retry attempts
without ever seeing a tool.

The mechanism: recall's MCP server loads fastembed before it can answer `initialize`. With no
memory to load it, Claude Code reports `{"name": "recall", "status": "failed"}` with an **empty
`mcp_server_errors`**, the session runs with no memory tools, the model answers from its own
knowledge, and the record looks perfectly ordinary. The admission gate catches it, correctly, and
discards the cell. So a starved host does not produce an error; it produces missing data.

**Why:** 8/72 is an 11.1% per-session startup failure rate. A paired cell is admitted only when
EVERY arm is wired, so an eight arm competitor grid carrying five memory servers admits a cell with
probability 0.889**5 = 0.55 if that rate holds and failures are independent, against an admission
rule of 95%. This is the binding constraint on widening the grid, not a tidiness issue.

pre-warmed HTTP transport instead of cold stdio. Handshake went 13.3 s to **458 ms**. That also
removes an unfairness nobody would have noticed: a cold start lands *inside* the treated arm's
measured wall time, so the benchmark charges the memory layer for an embedder load and calls it
retrieval overhead.

**The bill this produced.** Across the 112 agent A/B sessions with memory available, the agents
called exactly ONE tool, `recall_search`, 139 times. The other **seventeen were never invoked
once**. Over a 15-turn session that is roughly 39,000 input tokens per session for capability
nobody used. Scopes gate EXECUTION, not LISTING, so a read-only caller paid for the calibration
and ingest tools it was not allowed to call.

explicit names. Unset serves all 18, so no existing deployment changed. An unrecognised name
refuses to start, because a server silently serving a smaller surface than configured is
indistinguishable from an agent choosing not to call the missing tool.


hook still generates it as a fallback for worktrees made by hand with `git worktree add`, and for
those, expect the servers **one session later**. If a session needs recall's own corpus and the
servers are missing, do not debug the config; use the CLI, and check whether this checkout got its
file only just now.

symptom if you try is not an error about auth, it is `INDEX_NOT_READY: refused in strict trust mode

`build_auth` requires no mechanism and `RECALL_ENV=production` is free. The cost is a cold start
per session, measured at **9 s** for 981 chunks, almost all of it loading fastembed. That is only
affordable because Claude Code **2.1.221+ waits** for a pending MCP server; see

The corpus postgres listens on **127.0.0.1:55432 only**, and the memory and code tenants use hosted
Voyage models whose API key lives in VPS2's `.env`. Running the server on VPS2 puts the corpus, the
key and the models in one place: no tunnel, no API key copied onto the workstation, and
`.mcp.json` carries **no secret at all** because the command sources that `.env` on the far side.
`scripts/session-mcp.sh` generates it; `RECALL_VPS2_CHECKOUT` is the knob that has to move when the
corpus is migrated.

`re-call-docs` is off by default (`RECALL_MCP_INCLUDE_DOCS=1` enables it): bge-large is a local
ONNX model that goes resident in every stdio session on the host that also runs the live trading
services, while the other two load no model at all.

**Standing instruction from the user, given 2026-08-26, after having to repeat the go-ahead
roughly twenty sessions in a row: the VPS2 memory refresh is a session-close step. Run it. Do not
ask each time.** Cost of not having this memo: twenty sessions each stopping at "the indexer
refuses under production, ask before rebuilding a generation", each asking, each being told the
same thing.

**Why:** the corpus the MCP servers answer from is generation-bound (`recall_chunks_v1`, active
generation promoted at build time). Nothing incremental reaches it. Three shortcuts look like they
work and none do, each measured 2026-08-26 in one session:

1. `recall.cli --tenant memory index <path>` under `RECALL_ENV=development` runs green ("indexed
   250 chunks from 26 files") and writes the

⛔ **Do not grep transcripts for `mcp__<server>`.** Sessions *discuss* tool names, so the string
matches ordinary conversation. Measured: **4 of 6 transcripts contained `mcp__recall` while carrying
zero tools.** Three checks separate evidence from talk, in increasing strength:

1. count real `tool_use` blocks whose `name` starts with the prefix (strongest, but zero is
   uninformative: a session can have a tool and never call it, which is exactly what happened here);
2. require fully qualified names, `mcp__server__tool`, not the bare `mcp__server__` prefix;
3. **locate the record type**, and accept only `deferred_tools_delta`. This is the one that settles
   it.

Same family as the note in [[guards-that-cannot-fail]] about a checker matching the docstring that
mentions an exception, and [[probing-a-converter-with-a-renamed-file]].

## How to apply

Any question of the form "did that session have X available" is answerable retrospectively, for
**every** session on this machine, without starting anything. Prefer it to a live probe: it needs no
authentication, disturbs no other session's worktree, and yields n>1 immediately from history.

Used for `docs/preregistrations/2026-08-16-sessionstart-hook-mcp-ordering.md` (PR #392), which it
took from "unrunnable" to measured. Result and its caveats:
[[sessionstart-hook-cannot-load-its-own-mcp]].

⚠️ Do not conclude the tools are useless. Zero calls measures DISCOVERABILITY, not capability, and
the two have completely different fixes.

**Outcome-labeled in-context learning (ICL) with realized α as the label**.

## Concept 2 — SUPERSESSION AT WRITE-TIME (probably already done — validate + port)
Commenter's thesis (correct): timestamps fail because you're inferring a RELATION between two memos at read-time when both look valid in isolation. Supersession is not a property of a memo, it's a relation between two → a per-document freshness field can't catch it. Fix: capture the relation at WRITE-time — the new memo names what it replaces; retrieval returns the current head of the chain. Residual failure mode: depends on the writer's discipline (a missing link = an orphan memo that looks valid forever) — but a much better place to fail, because it's LINTABLE.
WORK: (a) verify the trust layer (#1899) implements exactly this; (b) build an eval that shows it catches a superseded-but-embedded memo a

you run it.

**How to apply:** after ANY edit to a file that documents cite, comments included, run the gate
before pushing. It is fast:

```bash
python -m pytest tests/test_doc_citations.py tests/test_citation_anchors.py -q
```

**Resolve by content, never by arithmetic.** `+3` was right both times here, and would have been
wrong the moment two edits landed in one file. Take the cited line's exact text from the commit
where it was correct and search for it in the new tree. When it is not unique (one of mine was a
bare `)` appearing twice, at 487 and 631), widen to a few lines of surrounding context until
exactly one match survives; a naive "closest to the expected offset" heuristic picks a plausible
wrong answer instead of failing.

| path | status |
|---|---|
| the prompt sent to the model | leak-free, verified across all 842 |
| submission rows | `task_id`, `Collection`, `input`, `contexts`, `predictions` only |
| the 65-task retrieval backfill | selected by **set difference on task ids**, never by label — reproduces on a sealed set |
| domain routing | uses `Collection`, which is provided |

🔑 **The distinction that matters is INFERENCE vs DIAGNOSIS.** Using the labels after a run to
stratify results is what they are for. Using them inside the system is the violation. The subtle
middle case is TUNING: a design decision motivated by a label-stratified analysis is not a leak,
but any gain it produced **cannot be claimed to transfer to the sealed set**, because the signal
that produced it will not be there.

query.query: A long running shared bash script fails at syntax that is not present in the file. What evidence suggests it was edited during execution?

pool.text:
**A bash script edited while a copy of it is running dies with a syntax error that is not in the
file.** bash reads script files lazily, by offset; a rewrite underneath a running instance shifts
the bytes so the parser resumes mid-line. Observed 2026-08-27: `refresh-memory.sh` failed with
``line 119: syntax error near unexpected token `do'`` on the text `sib in ...` (the `for ` sliced
off), while the file on disk had that line intact at line 105 and passed `bash -n` cleanly.
Another session's edit landed at 09:56:25, four seconds after the run started.

**How to apply:** when a long-running shared script dies with a syntax error, before touching the
file: (1) `bash -n` the file as it is now; (2) compare its mtime against the run's start time. A
clean parse plus an mtime inside the run's window means the script is healthy and the error was
the edit; rerun, repair nothing. Also read what the run completed before dying: in the observed
case the remote pipeline had already promoted and only the wrapper's local verification phase was
lost, so the "failure" needed a verification command, not a fix.

**So the file rule now has a second half, for scripted edits wherever they run:** assert the
anchor before replacing (`assert source.count(old) == 1`, not `>= 1`), and assert the result
differs from the input. A mechanical edit that cannot report a miss is an edit that silently does
nothing. The mutation harnesses in this session did carry that assertion, and it is what caught a
moved anchor cleanly instead of running twelve vacuous mutants.

See [[pasted-unicode-separators-rot]], [[audit-findings-need-reproducing]], and
[[guards-that-cannot-fail]], the same shape of failure, which is knowing the discipline and not
executing it.

My mutation harness reads `original = path.read_bytes()` when it applies each mutant and writes
those bytes back afterwards. Running it in the background and editing the same source file
during the run means the restore overwrites my edit with the pre-edit bytes. It happened
silently: no error, no conflict, and the reverted version went into the commit. I only noticed
because a later `Edit` failed to find the string I had written minutes earlier.

**Why:** the script's "restore" is a snapshot from its own start, not a diff, so it cannot tell
my edit from the mutation it applied.

⚠️ **A related trap the same day: a fork failure silently discarded an edit.** Under memory
pressure on this workstation, `bash` died with `dofork: child -1 ... Resource temporarily
unavailable`, killing a Python heredoc mid-script. The file was unchanged, the shell reported an
unrelated exit code, and nothing said the edit had not landed. **Read the file back after any
scripted edit on a loaded box**; use the Edit tool or PowerShell instead of a Bash heredoc once
forks start failing. See [[find-exec-semicolon-costs-a-fork-per-file]].

Cost: three red CI runs and three extra push cycles on work that was otherwise finished.

Related: [[a-served-tool-costs-153-tokens-every-turn]].

**Why it matters here:** the shared scripts under `~/.claude/recall-vps2/` and `~/.claude/hooks/`
are edited by concurrent sessions as a matter of course, and this failure pattern-matches to a
broken script, inviting a "fix" that reverts another session's fresh work.

Cost that bought it: none this time (diagnosed in minutes from the line-number mismatch); the
counterfactual was reverting a concurrent session's edit. Related:
[[git-bash-fork-failures-kill-scripts-silently]], [[memory-refresh-is-one-command-and-a-schedule]].

`/opt/sentiment_agent/.env` is authored as a **systemd EnvironmentFile**: values are NOT shell-quoted and may contain spaces / `:` / `+` (e.g. a timestamp `2026-05-29 12:00:00+00`). It is consumed by three readers — systemd `EnvironmentFile=`, python `utils.env_loader`, and shell wrappers — and the first two parse values literally (no execution).

**Why:** A bash `set -a; source "$APP_DIR/.env"` *executes* the file. An unquoted value with a space is split, and the trailing token is run as a command → `command not found`, exit 127. With `set -euo pipefail` this aborts the whole wrapper. This caused `sentiment-report.service` to fail at boot on 2026-05-29 (`run.sh:22`). It also means any `$(...)`/backtick in the secrets file would be *executed* — a real risk for a secrets file.

Observed 2026-08-23, TWICE in one session: an Edit to `recall/decision_ledger.py` meant to put
the six-character escape for U+0000 into a comment, and then the memo documenting that mistake
reproduced it in its own index line. Both times the tool-call JSON decoded the escape, so the
file received a literal NUL byte. Three symptoms,
none naming the cause: subsequent Edits failed with "string not found" though the text looked
identical, Read displayed empty backticks where the byte sat, and the module would have failed to
import (Python refuses source containing NUL) had it been executed before the repair.

**Why:** JSON interprets `\uXXXX` escapes in strings; a payload meant to SHOW an escape must not
spell it as one.

baseline_items.text:
**A bash script edited while a copy of it is running dies with a syntax error that is not in the
file.** bash reads script files lazily, by offset; a rewrite underneath a running instance shifts
the bytes so the parser resumes mid-line. Observed 2026-08-27: `refresh-memory.sh` failed with
``line 119: syntax error near unexpected token `do'`` on the text `sib in ...` (the `for ` sliced
off), while the file on disk had that line intact at line 105 and passed `bash -n` cleanly.
Another session's edit landed at 09:56:25, four seconds after the run started.

**How to apply:** when a long-running shared script dies with a syntax error, before touching the
file: (1) `bash -n` the file as it is now; (2) compare its mtime against the run's start time. A
clean parse plus an mtime inside the run's window means the script is healthy and the error was
the edit; rerun, repair nothing. Also read what the run completed before dying: in the observed
case the remote pipeline had already promoted and only the wrapper's local verification phase was
lost, so the "failure" needed a verification command, not a fix.

**So the file rule now has a second half, for scripted edits wherever they run:** assert the
anchor before replacing (`assert source.count(old) == 1`, not `>= 1`), and assert the result
differs from the input. A mechanical edit that cannot report a miss is an edit that silently does
nothing. The mutation harnesses in this session did carry that assertion, and it is what caught a
moved anchor cleanly instead of running twelve vacuous mutants.

My mutation harness reads `original = path.read_bytes()` when it applies each mutant and writes
those bytes back afterwards. Running it in the background and editing the same source file
during the run means the restore overwrites my edit with the pre-edit bytes. It happened
silently: no error, no conflict, and the reverted version went into the commit. I only noticed
because a later `Edit` failed to find the string I had written minutes earlier.

**Why:** the script's "restore" is a snapshot from its own start, not a diff, so it cannot tell
my edit from the mutation it applied.

## How to apply

* ⚠️ **The CLI path is NOT wired.** `recall/cli_commands/reasoning_cmd.py` on that branch contains
  no reference to `answer_provider` or `resolve_answer_provider`, so `recall reasoning query` still
  abstains from the command line. Only `recall_mcp/server.py` resolves it. Anyone verifying through
  the CLI will read a working integration as broken.
* **`max_model_calls=0` was never the blocker**, contrary to what I told the user. The answer call

# Validation Standards

Every backtest needs: bootstrap CI + permutation test + Holm-Bonferroni correction (primary multiple-hypothesis gate, alpha=0.05) + out-of-sample period >= 1 year. Bonferroni and Sidak may be reported as audit comparisons; BH-FDR is exploratory/legacy and must not be the sole promotion criterion. Walk-forward for time-series.

Month-of-year effects: require N>=3 years before trusting. Always test SPY-only to separate alpha from calendar beta.

Top-1% / top-5% buckets are often **toxic** (recurring pattern -- see short vol v2, Meta-Stacker A v4). Don't promote on top-bucket performance alone.

See also: [[feedback_holm_bonferroni_primary]] and [[feedback_evaluate_by_expectancy_not_winrate]].

# What this records

Authenticated MCP mutations now persist their completed response in the PostgreSQL audit table
before attempting Redis response caching. A retry whose Redis marker exists but whose Redis result
is missing checks the tenant scoped PostgreSQL receipt and replays it. If both stores lack the
response, the server returns `reconciliation_required` and does not execute the mutation again.

The receipt identity is a SHA 256 derived event ID, so the client idempotency key is not written to
the audit table. Keep the PostgreSQL receipt lookup and the Redis cache write in this order when
changing mutation response handling.

# What this records

Commit `595daac5` adds `test_bootstrap_does_not_mutate_the_real_process_environment` in
`tests/test_settings.py`. The test configures an approved secret mapping in the real process
environment, snapshots `dict(os.environ)`, bootstraps with a fake provider, and asserts both that
the resolved value reaches the settings snapshot and that the process environment is identical
afterward.

Why it matters: writing the resolved secret to `os.environ` would leak it into later operations and
child processes. The test was shown red with a deliberate double assignment to `os.environ` at the
secret assignment line, failing at the environment equality assertion, then restored and shown
green. Apply the same process environment snapshot whenever bootstrap secret destinations change.

**(a) The signature is hardware, not intrusion.** The decisive fact is already above: **the Rescue
System also failed to boot.** Rescue netboots the *provider's* image and never touches your volume,
so an attacker holding root inside the VM has no mechanism to stop it. Supporting tells all point the
same way: boot hangs *before* root is mounted (the block device is missing, not wiped); `Input/output
error` on `/usr/bin/tail` and `bad marshal data` on an unrelated `.pyc` are **random read corruption
across arbitrary files**, which is a failing device, not malware (malware corrupts purposefully); and
there is no ransom note or contact. 🔑 **A wiper leaves a bootable empty system. A dead volume leaves
no volume — and cannot break the provider's rescue image.**

**Incident:** postgres (`postgresql@16-main`, VPS3) crashed into automatic recovery

`NRestarts=0`). It sat **REFUSING connections for ~3.5h** (02:14→05:46), so the ENTIRE
trading stack errored `OperationalError: connection refused` (~9k errors: updown,

An audit finding said `scripts/task_admission.py` gated the BASELINE arm's rate by
`MIN_SESSIONS = 6` and did not gate the BEST arm's, while both fed the same verdict. The obvious
symmetry fix is to gate both. **That fix was wrong, and it passed everything.**

`FLOOR` is defined by its own comment as "a task NO arm has ever solved". That is an **existence**
test. Gating it by session count silently turns it into a **rate** test: "no arm with at least six
sessions has a rate above zero". Three tasks flipped from BENEFIT-ONLY to FLOOR because their only
successes came from `oracle_memory`, which carries 3 sessions:

| task | oracle_memory | every other arm |
|---|---|---|
| ts-empty-input | 1/3 | 0 of 47 |
| ts-log-mask | **3/3** | 0 of 56 |
| ts-retry-cap | 1/3 | 0 of 55 |

Separately, `p50/p95/p99` were reported one rank too high (`int(q*n)` used as a 0-based index *is*
the 1-based nearest rank): p99 of 100 samples returned the max. Two copies of the formula, both
wrong. The fix moves a percentile by exactly one rank when `q*n` is an integer and is a no-op
otherwise — it does **not** explain the swings above.

`401 Invalid api key`. Root cause was NOT creds (SDK canary PLACED+cancelled a
real order with the racers' identity → account trade-capable; env creds ==
freshly-derived, all match). It was `copytrade_racer::load_submitter`: sent the
**FUNDER** (`RACER_MAKER_ADDRESS`) as `POLY_ADDRESS` + read passphrase from the
WRONG env (`RACER_PASSPHRASE` vs actual `RACER_API_PASSPHRASE` → empty). Polymarket
L2 auth needs `POLY_ADDRESS` = the **signer** (api-key owner `0xa364b3C6…`, NOT
funder `0x5307…`). updown_lag_racer already had this fix (commit `1b248135`
2026-06-27) — the newer copytrade crate never got it. **Fix (#1599, MERGED+DEPLOYED):**

- **DD checks are already blind during stale**: `floating_pnl ≈ 0` ⇒ `equity ≈ balance` ⇒ DD reports 0. Old `close_all` was acting on no better information than new `block-only` behavior — just more destructively.

pool.text:
**The base rate is why, and it was registered before measuring: the memo was needed in 11 of 48
sessions, 23%.** A mechanism firing on every write, where three quarters of sessions need nothing,
is mostly firing when nothing is wrong. No gate changes that arithmetic.

**Registered cell: KILL the per-write design.** What survives is the query formulation — using the
code about to be saved rather than the task description, worth 11/11 against 1/14 — and the
remaining shape is a search the agent asks for DELIBERATELY, which needs no trigger because it has
no trigger problem. That is unregistered, and its endpoint would have to be task success, since
"the agent chose to search" cannot be measured by replaying recorded sessions.

🔑 **Draft-time search finds the memo in EVERY session that actually needed it**, which retires the
6-to-10 judge range: on the question that matters (did the agent fall into the trap, would the memo
have reached it) the answer is all of them.

⛔ **And it fires on 29 of 36 sessions that demonstrably did not need it. The mechanism works
perfectly and cannot be aimed.** The best gate found across four registered attempts moves false
fires 0.806 → 0.722 while costing one of the eleven: a 10% cut in noise for a 9% cut in the thing
that works.

a per-write LLM gate is dominated on every axis at far higher cost. Verdict GATE, and the 18-draft negative set is the binding limit on the lane.

**Why it is dangerous rather than merely annoying.** It fails with **exit code 0** and returns a
smaller, plausible number. A regex written `[\\/]` arrives as `[\/]`, which matches a forward slash
only, so it silently stops matching every Windows path. In the audit that found this, a probe
counting sessions that hand-read memory files reported **2 where the true answer was 164**, and the
run looked clean. The apparatus was corrupt and did not say so. ↔ [[feedback-predict-before-measuring-and-assert-the-invariant-2026-07-27]]

**The fix is always the same:** the **Write tool preserves backslashes exactly** (verified in the
same session). Put the script in a file, then run the file. Never inline a regex or a Windows path
in a shell command.

**So the retrieval-side lane is finished** (four generation-side attempts, one threshold frontier,
one fusion frontier). What remains is only about WHEN to ask: a **trigger** that decides which
writes deserve a search using something other than the retrieval score, or accepting the noise and
measuring task success directly. Neither is licensed; both need their own registration, and the
second should note this project already measured a task-success null
([[agent-ab-task-success-result-2026-08-22]]).

Landed 2026-08-09 in `d8f4f57`, "Add first install wizard and calibration setup". Code is
`recall/setup.py` (`run_setup_wizard`), tests are `tests/test_setup.py`.

The command is `recall setup`. It was designed under the name "recall init" in the spec (#249) and
implementation plan (#250), but no `init` subcommand was ever registered, and both of those
documents were deleted from the tree by #262 in the docs reorganization. So the old name survives

What it actually does:

🔑 **A dumb string-membership test beat the LLM gate on every axis, at a fraction of the cost.**
The vocabulary test is: extract identifier-like tokens from the corpus, keep those appearing in at
most two memos (distinctive), and search only when the draft contains one. No model call, a set
lookup per write. I predicted the LLM gate would win precisely because it "reasons about the code
rather than matching strings"; it was dominated by matching strings. **When the signal you need is
literally a shared identifier, a model adds cost and judgement where neither was the missing
ingredient.**

| I read | It actually is | What it looked like |
|---|---|---|
| `payload["results"]` | `payload["hits"]` | recall returned **0 results** while reporting `trust_state: trusted` — a certified corpus answering nothing |
| `record["metadata"]["memory_call_count"]` | top-level `record["memory_call_count"]` | recall's **search rate 0.000** across every arm, which would have voided the run under prediction 1's floor |
| `json.loads(output)` | output is `{"result": "<escaped json string>"}`, needs decoding **twice** | every recall search returned **zero hits**, i.e. retrieval completely dead |

Every one produced a confident, coherent, alarming negative about the product. I was one step from
reporting the second as "the run is void" and the third as "retrieval is broken".

**Why it works, and it is not subtle.** A draft contains the literal identifiers the memo's fix
line contains. One `ts-lf-rewrite` session wrote `version_file.write_text(content,
encoding="utf-8")`; the memo says `path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")`. That is
a lexical match no amount of prose rewriting could manufacture, and it exists only in the artifact,
never in the goal. "You cannot look up a hazard you do not know exists" is true of the goal and
FALSE of the draft: the draft already contains the operation that will fail.

turned the Claude Code hook into an automatic indexer. Against VPS2 that is wrong on the user's

It was already fail-safe rather than fail-wrong, and that was measured rather than assumed:

`RuntimeError: VoyageEmbedder needs VOYAGE_API_KEY (env) or an explicit api_key`, because

directly, so the key sitting in the repo's `.env` never reaches it. Re-measure:

⚠️ **Read the ACTIONABLE column, not the retrieved one.** See the correction below: retrieval and
applicability are different, and this memo published the wrong one first.

`ts-lf-rewrite`, which resisted four registered attempts 0 for 6, is **6 of 6** at ranks 1,1,1,1,1,3.

🔑 **The diagnosis this settles: retrieval was never the problem, the MOMENT of the query was.**
The same fused retriever ranks the governing memo **127 to 142** for the session's goal query and
**1** for its draft. `goal_fused` reaches 14/14 by k=200, so every memo was always present and
findable at a depth no consumer reads. Four generation-side attempts tried to move the DOCUMENT
toward the query (see
[[authored-discoverability-surfaces-cannot-close-the-formulation-gap]]); the document was fine.

**Why:** CLAUDE.md's rule is explicit — *"before answering 'have we done/tested X?', before
re-proposing a hypothesis, run `docs_search(source_type='memory', …)` BEFORE grepping or reading

Mutating the guard proves the assertion runs against the code. It says nothing about whether the
assertion runs at all.

Two cases that week survived every mutation and were caught only by a second platform in CI: a test
that created the directory it was comparing case-insensitively (so Windows `resolve()` collapsed
both spellings before the comparison), and a test whose "two spellings" were `str(p)` and
`p.as_posix()`, identical on POSIX, so the fixture held one key. In both, the mutation died against
an assertion that was never running.

So the rule here is necessary and not sufficient. The additions are in
[[one-test-must-cross-the-seam]]: assert the fixture is non-degenerate before deriving anything from
it, and let exactly one test per seam reach the real file or process.

baseline_items.text:
**The base rate is why, and it was registered before measuring: the memo was needed in 11 of 48
sessions, 23%.** A mechanism firing on every write, where three quarters of sessions need nothing,
is mostly firing when nothing is wrong. No gate changes that arithmetic.

**Registered cell: KILL the per-write design.** What survives is the query formulation — using the
code about to be saved rather than the task description, worth 11/11 against 1/14 — and the
remaining shape is a search the agent asks for DELIBERATELY, which needs no trigger because it has
no trigger problem. That is unregistered, and its endpoint would have to be task success, since
"the agent chose to search" cannot be measured by replaying recorded sessions.

🔑 **Draft-time search finds the memo in EVERY session that actually needed it**, which retires the
6-to-10 judge range: on the question that matters (did the agent fall into the trap, would the memo
have reached it) the answer is all of them.

⛔ **And it fires on 29 of 36 sessions that demonstrably did not need it. The mechanism works
perfectly and cannot be aimed.** The best gate found across four registered attempts moves false
fires 0.806 → 0.722 while costing one of the eleven: a 10% cut in noise for a 9% cut in the thing
that works.

⚠️ Six of the seven quiet negatives are `ts-raise-on-missing`, whose memo is the one
reconstruction-approximate source in the corpus. Strip those and the mechanism is silent on 1 of 30
sessions that did not need it.

Related: [[hazard-query-instruction-result-2026-08-23]] (the misses), [[check-memory-before-acting]]
if that skill is ever revised, since this is the concrete correction to its query advice.

exists in the official CLI but is only read by the `vllm` provider, which is why a patch is needed

🔑 **The count alone is not the signal; the count of generations OLDER THAN the retention floor is.**
That number was zero, which is a healthy pipeline, not a stalled one. `CLAUDE.md`'s own sentence
already implies this ("the age floor dominates the count, so `--retention-days` is the knob that
bounds growth"), and I quoted the heuristic without applying the qualifier one line below it.

**How to apply:** before reporting a gc backlog, get the AGES, not the count:

```
== 6/6 generation gc (keep active + previous + 1 more retired; 2-day age floor) ==
collected 0 generation(s): (none)
```

and the count still went **14 → 15**. Two different conditions produce the identical symptom:

| condition | `retired: N` | `collected` line |
|---|---|---|
| gc never ran | climbs | **absent from the log** |
| gc ran, the age floor protected everything | climbs | `collected 0 generation(s)` |

🔑 **The distinguishing evidence is the `collected` line, not the count.** A count is a level; only
the log says whether the step executed. This is the same shape as
[[a-recorded-number-nobody-compares-is-not-a-check]]: a number that is recorded faithfully and
means two opposite things depending on something nobody reads.

What the run reported, in one pass: `--check` printed `retired: 27 retired/failed
generation(s) awaiting gc`, and then step 6 printed `collected 0 generation(s): (none)`. Those
two lines look contradictory and are both correct. The generations table says why:

```text
state    n   under_48h  oldest               newest
retired  28  27         2026-08-24 21:01:54  2026-08-27 13:58:12
active    1   1         2026-08-27 15:49:47  2026-08-27 15:49:47
```

27 of the 28 retired generations are inside the 48-hour age floor, and the 1 that is not is
held by retain-previous. So gc had nothing it was permitted to collect, and collected nothing.

`CLAUDE.md` says a retired-generation count in double digits and climbing means step 6 has stopped
running. I read 11 that way, flagged it to the user as a broken pipeline, and was wrong.

The measurement that corrected it, and the one to take before repeating the claim:

| generation | age | rows |
|---|---:|---:|
| r57 | 46.5h | 10,238 |
| r58 - r64 | 42.2h to 5.8h | ~10.3k each |
| r65 - r67 | 2.1h to 0.8h | ~10.5k each |

**All eleven were younger than 48 hours**, so with the pipeline's own `--retention-days 2` the age
floor protected every one and `gc` correctly collected zero (`collected 0 generation(s): (none)`,
exit 0). The count was high because this corpus churns several generations a day, and on that day
the hourly task promoted four.

Read step 6's own `collected N` line instead, which is the direct observation. `retired: N` is
worth reading only when N greatly exceeds twice the recent build rate, or when the oldest
retired generation is well past the age floor.

"no memo records this (searched: memory corpus)" is true and useful. "No prior work exists" is a
claim about the repository and needs a repository search.

repo, `git grep` / `rg` the repo too. Cheapest sufficient check for an invariant: grep `tests/` for
the identifier or the concept before concluding it is uncovered.

artefact contain a thing I have a standing rule against", the prior is ZERO, not a small number.**

claim about the repository and needs a repository search.

repo, `git grep` / `rg` the repo too. Cheapest sufficient check for an invariant: grep `tests/` for
the identifier or the concept before concluding it is uncovered.

re-proposing a hypothesis, run `docs_search(source_type='memory', …)` BEFORE grepping or reading
memo files by hand."* I went straight to designing experiments. The memory corpus is indexed and
the search takes seconds.

project has already spent measurement budget.

⛔ **`hf upload` CANNOT update the Space, and the error does not say so.** It returns
**402 Payment Required** on `api/repos/create` with the message *"hosting Gradio and Docker
Spaces on free cpu-basic requires a PRO subscription"*, which reads as a billing problem with the
account. It is not. `hf upload` always issues a create-if-missing call, and that call defaults to
a non-static SDK, so it is refused **even though the Space already exists and is `sdk: static`**.
There is no `--space-sdk` flag on `hf upload` to fix it.

What works, because `upload_folder` does not create:

```python

HfApi().upload_folder(folder_path="build/hf/space",
                      repo_id="Gde05/agent-memory-bench", repo_type="space")
```

1. **`short_description` is capped at 60 characters**, and the API validates README frontmatter
   BEFORE uploading anything, so one long line aborts the whole folder with `Invalid metadata in
   README.md`.
2. **`hf upload` has no `--space-sdk` option** (checked against `huggingface_hub` 1.24.0), so the
   CLI cannot create a Space with the right SDK. `HfApi().create_repo(..., repo_type='space',
   space_sdk='static')` can, so the "make it in the web UI first" step is optional, not required.
3. **Creating a static Space leaves a stub `style.css`.** The site ships `styles.css`, so the stub
   is dead weight that survives an `upload_folder`, which overwrites rather than mirrors. Deleted
   by hand.

Re-running a failed check on a PR (`gh run rerun <id> --failed`, or the GitHub "Re-run failed
jobs" button) **replays the same commit SHA** it originally built. For a `pull_request` event that
SHA is the *merge commit computed when the event fired*, i.e. head + base **as base stood then**.

Consequence: when a job fails for a reason that was fixed **on the base branch afterwards**, a
re-run **fails again, identically**, and the identical error reads as "my fix did not work".

The repair is to make GitHub compute a **new** merge commit:

```bash
gh pr update-branch <pr>     # == the "Update branch" button
```

🔑 **A re-run answers "was this flaky?", never "is this fixed on base?"** Reach for `update-branch`
whenever the fix landed somewhere other than the PR's own head.
